0.title: The Letter of Joy: Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
0.overview:
The message. Philippians is a letter of friendship and joy, written by a prisoner to the church that had stood beside him longest. Its message is that Christ is enough: enough to make a prisoner glad and calm, and enough to make a quarrelling church one. “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (1:21). The words “joy” and “rejoice” come some sixteen times in four short chapters: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice” (4:4). This is not the forced cheerfulness of denial but the settled gladness of a man who has found Christ sufficient, even facing death.

Background: the writer. The letter comes from Paul and Timothy (1:1), though Paul speaks in his own voice, and hardly anyone doubts that he wrote it. He writes as a prisoner awaiting a verdict that could mean release or death (1:19–26; 2:23–24). Where was he held? Some argue for Ephesus, near enough to Philippi for the several journeys the letter implies, though Acts records no imprisonment there; others for Caesarea, where Paul was held for two years (Acts 24:27). The more likely answer is Rome, during his house arrest of about AD 60–62 (Acts 28:16, 30–31), under Nero. Paul mentions “the whole imperial guard” (1:13) and “those of Caesar’s household” (4:22), and he faces a case with no further appeal, which fits Rome, where he had appealed to Caesar, best. Little of the letter’s teaching depends on the answer.

Philippi. Philippi lay in eastern Macedonia, in what is now northern Greece, on the main Roman road to the East. It was named after Philip II, father of Alexander the Great. In 42 BC Mark Antony and Octavian, later Caesar Augustus, defeated the assassins of Julius Caesar outside the city, and Rome refounded it as a colony settled by veteran soldiers: “a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony” (Acts 16:12). A colony was a little Rome abroad, proud of its Roman citizenship, Roman law and Roman magistrates, where the emperor was honoured as lord and saviour. So Paul tells this church to “let your manner of life be worthy of the gospel” (1:27), using a word that means to live as citizens, and reminds them, “But our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ” (3:20).

Paul and the church there. Paul came about AD 49 or 50, on his second journey, after a vision of a man of Macedonia pleading, “Come over to Macedonia and help us” (Acts 16:9). It was his first church in Europe. With him were Silas, Timothy and probably Luke. At a place of prayer by the river the first convert was Lydia, a seller of purple goods and a worshipper of God. A slave girl was freed from a spirit of divination; her owners, robbed of their income, had Paul and Silas beaten and jailed as Jews who “advocate customs that are not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice” (Acts 16:21); at midnight an earthquake shook the prison, and the jailer believed. From these unlikely beginnings came Paul’s most faithful supporters: “no church entered into partnership with me in giving and receiving, except you only” (4:15). They sent help to Thessalonica more than once (4:16). Now they had “overseers and deacons” (1:1), and they too were suffering for Christ (1:29–30).

What prompted the letter. Hearing of Paul’s imprisonment, the church sent Epaphroditus with a gift (4:18). He fell ill, “near to death” (2:27), and now Paul sends him home with this letter. It honours him (2:25–30), thanks the church, delicately, for its gift (4:10–20), gives news of Paul’s case (1:12–26), and meets three dangers: opponents outside (1:27–30); rivalry and grumbling inside, which had come to a head between Euodia and Syntyche (2:1–4; 4:2–3); and teachers who insisted that Gentile believers must be circumcised (3:2–3). The sharp change of tone at 3:2 has led some scholars to think the letter joins two or three of Paul’s notes, but no manuscript shows it in any other form, and this commentary reads it as one letter.

How the letter makes its case. Chapter 1 opens with thanksgiving and prayer for the Philippians (1:1–11), then reports from prison: Paul’s chains have advanced the gospel, and by life or by death Christ will be honoured (1:12–26); it ends with a call to stand together as citizens worthy of the gospel (1:27–30). Chapter 2 sets before them the mind of Christ, who emptied himself and was obedient to death on a cross, and whom God has highly exalted (2:1–11); then the consequences (2:12–18) and two living examples, Timothy and Epaphroditus (2:19–30). Chapter 3 is a warning and a testimony: Paul counts his credentials as a Pharisee, blameless under the law, as loss, “rubbish” (the Greek word is coarser), beside “the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (3:8); yet he has not arrived, but presses on like a runner toward the prize (3:12–21). Chapter 4 gathers the threads into practice: unity, joy, prayer in place of anxiety, a mind set on what is good (4:1–9), and thanks from a man who has learned contentment (4:10–23). One pattern runs through it all: Christ, and then Paul, Timothy and Epaphroditus, each setting aside his own interests for others.

Where it leads: to Christ. The heart of the letter is 2:6–11, which many think was an early hymn already known in the churches. It follows the Son from the form of God, down through becoming man to a slave’s death on a cross, and up to the exaltation at which “every knee should bow” and “every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord” (2:10–11). Those words come from Isaiah 45:23, where the LORD says, “To me every knee shall bow”; Paul gives them to Jesus. He did not stop being God when he emptied himself: he took a servant’s form without laying aside his deity. And the hymn is pattern as well as praise: “Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus” (2:5). In chapter 3 the same Christ is the believer’s whole standing before God, found in him, “not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ” (3:9), and the Saviour who will “transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body” (3:21). In a city that hailed the emperor as lord and saviour, Philippians gives both titles to Jesus.

For us. Philippians shows what a life shaped by the gospel looks like: partnership rather than rivalry, humility rather than self-promotion, contentment rather than anxiety, pressing forward rather than dwelling on the past, and the peace of God, “which surpasses all understanding” (4:7), rather than a security resting on circumstances. It does not shame the anxious; it tells them where to take their cares. It calls us to work at holiness because God is at work in us, and promises that “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (1:6). And it comes from a man in chains who could look at death and say, “My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better” (1:23).

1.title: To Live Is Christ: Partnership, Prison, and the Advance of the Gospel
1.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 opens Paul’s letter of thanks from prison: greeting and prayer, news of how things stand with him, and the one command the rest of the letter unpacks.

The message. Christ is enough, in prison and in death. A man in chains can be glad, because God finishes what he starts, because chains and even rivals only spread the name of Christ, and because for one whose life is Christ, death is not loss but gain. And a church that shares that confidence can stand together, unafraid, as citizens of heaven in a city that belongs to Caesar.

Why it was said. The Philippians were anxious for their apostle, whose trial could end in execution; they faced opposition of their own, and they were beginning to quarrel (see the introduction). Had the gospel stalled now that its leading preacher was locked up? Paul answers with news, prayer and a call to courage.

How the chapter makes its case. Paul thanks God for their partnership in the gospel, is sure God will complete his work in them, and prays that their love will grow in discernment until the day of Christ (vv. 1–11). His imprisonment has carried the gospel into the imperial guard and made others bold, and even rivals who want to hurt him are spreading the message, so he rejoices (vv. 12–18). Facing life or death, he wants only that Christ be honoured in his body; he would rather depart and be with Christ, but expects to stay for their sake (vv. 19–26). Then he turns to them: live as citizens worthy of the gospel, side by side and unafraid, for believing in Christ and suffering for him are both gifts of grace (vv. 27–30).

Where it leads. Over the whole chapter stands one name: Christ, whom Paul serves, whose affection runs through him, whom even his rivals proclaim, and whom he longs to be with. “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (v. 21) is the secret of the joy, the calm, the generosity towards rivals and the willingness to stay. And behind Paul’s choice to stay for others lies the greater choice of the next chapter: the Son who left his glory for people who needed him.

For us. Fill in the blank honestly: for to me to live is what? Then look at the circumstance you would most like to change, ask who is watching you in it, and how Christ might be honoured there.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul’s thanks and prayer rest on one conviction: what God begins in his people, he finishes. He greets the whole church as saints in Christ (vv. 1–2), thanks God with joy for their partnership in the gospel from the first day (vv. 3–5), and is sure that God will complete his work in them at the day of Christ (v. 6). His love for them is Christ’s own affection, shared even in his chains (vv. 7–8), and he prays that their love will grow in knowledge and discernment, so that they are ready for that day, full of the fruit that comes through Jesus Christ (vv. 9–11).
verseByVerse.theology:
The God Who Finishes What He Starts

The force of Philippians 1:6 lies in who does the two actions. God began the good work; God will complete it. The believer is the field being worked, not the farmer doing the work. This does not make effort pointless (2:12–13), and assurance rests on his grip, not ours (see the note on v. 6).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Philippians had reasons for anxiety: their apostle was in chains, their city was a Roman garrison town where the imperial cult was a civic expectation, opposition was real (v. 28), and the congregation had a quarrel in it (4:2). Paul points them to the God who started the work.

Now: Verse 9 supplies the prayer to pray for the people you love (see the note on vv. 9–11).

verseByVerse.quote: Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, To all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the overseers and deacons: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two servants of Christ greet the whole church as saints, and give them grace and peace from the Father and the Son. In a few words it says who Christians are: servants of Christ, holy in him, receivers of grace.

Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus. Paul’s first word about himself is douloi, slaves, not “apostle”. He claims that title when his authority is under attack; with a church that loves him and needs no persuading, he leaves it aside. The word he chooses instead is the one he will use of Christ in the letter’s great hymn: Jesus emptied himself, “by taking the form of a servant” (2:7). Before Paul asks the Philippians to have the mind of Christ, he shows them a man who has begun to have it. A slave in that world owned nothing, not even his time; Paul and Timothy wear that status as a title, because their Master first took it on himself.

To all the saints in Christ Jesus. Holy ones (hagioi): not a rank for exceptional godliness, nor a report on how they are doing, but a statement of where they are: in Christ Jesus. To be in Christ is to be joined to him by faith, so that his standing before God becomes yours: his death counts as your death to sin, his risen life is your new life, and his righteousness covers you (Romans 6:4–5; 2 Corinthians 5:21). The church in Philippi (see the introduction) had nothing in common but him: Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth whose heart the Lord opened (Acts 16:14); a slave girl delivered from the spirit that made her somebody’s income (Acts 16:16–18); and the jailer who fastened Paul and Silas in the stocks and then washed their wounds (Acts 16:33). Over them all God writes the same name. Nothing about them made it so; everything about him does.

The word “all”. Paul says it again and again (1:4, 7, 8, 25), in a letter that must eventually name two women who cannot get along (4:2). He will not let any party in the church imagine he belongs to them more than to the others.

Two addresses. Paul writes both on the envelope: in Christ Jesus, and at Philippi. The first is where they live; the second is where they are stationed. The first does not change if they move house or are driven out of the city, and decides who they are; the second is where they show it, in that street, with those neighbours. A Christian who forgets the first becomes anxious and worldly; one who forgets the second becomes otherworldly and useless.

With the overseers and deacons. No other letter of Paul greets the church’s officers in the address. The overseers (episkopoi, from which comes the word bishop) were the elders who led and taught (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5–7); the deacons (diakonoi, servants) served the church’s practical needs (1 Timothy 3:8–13). Two offices, both plural. Paul greets the whole body first and its leaders second, in the same sentence: the officers are not over the saints but among them. They may have organised the gift Epaphroditus brought (4:18), which would explain the mention.

Grace to you and peace. The order never varies in Paul, and cannot. Grace is God’s unearned favour reaching down; peace is what that favour creates when it lands: not a mood, but the end of the war (Romans 5:1). Much religion tries to produce peace of mind without first settling whether God has shown us his favour, and it cannot be done. Both come from the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ together, one source, one gift: Paul names the Son beside the Father without a pause. A man in chains begins by giving away the two things no prison can confiscate.

Why is Timothy named, if Paul wrote the letter? Timothy joined Paul just before the church was founded and was very probably there (Acts 16:1–3, 12; 17:14); the Philippians loved him, and Paul is about to send him to them (2:19–23). Naming him shows that the letter comes from the gospel team, not one celebrated man. But he is co-sender, not co-author: from verse 3 Paul writes as “I”, and in chapter 2 speaks of Timothy in the third person. And Paul calls them both servants: the older apostle and his younger helper stand on the same footing before Christ.

Am I a saint if I do not feel holy? Yes, if you are in Christ. Saint is not a feeling or an achievement but what God has made you by joining you to his Son (1 Corinthians 1:2, 30); the Corinthians were called saints in the same letter that rebuked their quarrels and immorality. But the name is also a calling, and the rest of this letter shows what it looks like: humble, joyful, united, pressing on. You do not become a saint by living a holy life. You live a holy life because you are one.

What do elders and deacons actually do, and how should I treat them? Elders shepherd the church: they teach the word, pray, watch over souls and give account to God for them (Acts 20:28; Hebrews 13:17; 1 Peter 5:1–4). Deacons serve the body’s practical needs so that the word is not neglected: the poor and sick, money and property, and much quiet work that keeps a congregation running (Acts 6:1–6). Respect and love them (1 Thessalonians 5:12–13), pray for them, make their work a joy and not a groan, and bring concerns to them directly and graciously, not behind their backs. They are not above correction; nor are they your staff.

Where Christians differ: church government. Some churches have a bishop over many congregations, distinct from elders; others have a single pastor with no elders. Episcopal churches see the bishop as a later and legitimate development, pointing to the wider roles of Timothy and Titus, and Presbyterian churches share the plurality of elders but join congregations under wider courts. This commentary’s view: in the New Testament, overseer and elder are the same office: Paul calls the Ephesian elders (Acts 20:17) overseers (Acts 20:28), and uses both words of the same men in Titus 1:5–7. Each church was led not by one man but by a plurality of qualified men, with deacons serving alongside: two offices, with elders sharing leadership. Churches may organise their wider fellowship in various ways, and godly believers in other traditions serve Christ faithfully, but this local pattern is biblical.
verseByVerse.note: Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, the first church Paul founded in Europe. He wrote from prison, probably in Rome. “Overseers” (elders) and deacons were the two offices of leadership.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank my God in all my remembrance of you, always in every prayer of mine for you all making my prayer with joy, because of your partnership in the gospel from the first day until now.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul thanks God with joy for the Philippians, because from the first day they have been his partners in the gospel. The thanks go to God, not to them, because everything good in them is his work (v. 6).

In all my remembrance of you. All of it, with no memory set aside. Paul had been beaten with rods in this city and put in the stocks, and he knew this church’s quarrels (4:2). Yet there is no memory of Philippi that he has to step around in order to give thanks.

Making my prayer with joy. Joy (chara) appears here for the first time in a letter where joy and rejoicing come back some sixteen times, from a man in chains. Prayer for others, often a duty, is here Paul’s delight, and thanks comes before request.

Your partnership in the gospel. The word is koinōnia: sharing, going in together on a venture. In ordinary Greek it could describe a business partnership, two men with capital in the same ship, and that is nearer Paul’s meaning than warm feeling. The Philippians had put money into the gospel enterprise from the start (4:15–16), and themselves too: their prayers, their messenger, their own suffering. They were not Paul’s audience or his donors but shareholders in the same undertaking.

What it cost them. Philippi was not a wealthy church. Of the Macedonian churches, Philippi surely among them, Paul tells Corinth that in a severe test of affliction their joy and deep poverty overflowed in a wealth of generosity: they gave beyond their means, of their own accord, begging earnestly to take part (2 Corinthians 8:1–5). Poor people who begged to give more than they could afford: that is the koinōnia Paul thanks God for, a decade later.

From the first day until now. The first day was a riverbank and a handful of praying women, and Lydia’s first act as a believer was to open her house (Acts 16:15). Between that day and this lie an earthquake, a jail, a magistrate’s apology, and years of gifts carried up and down the Egnatian Way. History matters between Christians: a friendship that has cost something and survived is not a new acquaintance.

Partners because first partakers. Their partnership with Paul rested on a deeper one: God had called them into the fellowship, the koinōnia, of his Son (1 Corinthians 1:9). The gospel is not first a cause to support but Christ sharing himself with sinners: his righteousness, his Spirit, his Father, his inheritance. The Macedonians gave themselves first to the Lord and then to Paul (2 Corinthians 8:5), and that order explains their generosity. The Son brought the whole capital into this venture, his own life. He opened Lydia’s heart before she opened her door, every coin carried to Paul was his gift to the giver first, and still he counts the smallest share that poor people put in beside his.

What if there are people in my church I cannot thank God for? Begin where Paul begins, with what God has done. If they are in Christ, God has begun a good work in them (v. 6), and you can thank him for that before you can thank him for their manner. Name one thing in them that is plainly his grace, however small, their faithfulness in turning up, their love for their children, a gift they use, and thank God for it specifically. Thanksgiving does not pretend there are no faults (Paul deals frankly with a quarrel in chapter 4), but it changes how you see them; it is very hard to go on resenting someone you thank God for every week.

How can I be a partner in the gospel if I have little to give? The Philippians were poor, and they are the model: partnership is measured by sharing, not size. Pray by name for gospel workers, and tell them you do. Give what you can, proportionately and gladly (2 Corinthians 9:7). Open your home. Write to someone labouring in a hard place. Stand with believers who suffer. Above all, live and speak the gospel where you are. The widow’s two coins (Mark 12:41–44) were counted in heaven as the largest gift in the treasury.
verseByVerse.note: The Philippians had supported Paul financially from the start.

verseByVerse.quote: And I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God finishes what he starts: the work he began in these believers he will complete on the day Christ returns. Paul’s confidence is not that the Philippians will finish what they started, but that God will finish what he started.

And I am sure of this. “Sure” (pepoithōs) means persuaded, settled. Both actions that follow, began (enarxamenos) and will bring to completion (epitelesei), are God’s. A work God begins in a person is not an experiment, and he is not a builder who runs out of money at the second storey.

A good work in you. The whole of it: the moment you first believed, the verdict of not guilty pronounced over you in Christ, and the slow making new that goes on now, usually more visible to others than to you. In Philippi it began with a heart opened at a riverbank (Acts 16:14) and a jailer asking what he must do to be saved (Acts 16:30); neither of them started it. And it includes their partnership in the gospel (v. 5): their generosity was his work too.

At the day of Jesus Christ. The finish line is named: not the day you die, nor the day you finally get on top of the sin that has beaten you for thirty years, but the day he appears and transforms our lowly body to be like his glorious body (3:21). God is making you like his Son (Romans 8:29), and the work is complete when you see him, for when he appears we shall be like him (1 John 3:2).

His grip, not ours. The believer who lies awake asking whether he will still be a Christian in twenty years is asking about his own grip, and if the answer lay there, the honest reply would be: probably not. This verse answers a different question, whether God will let go, and its answer is “I am sure of this”. Paul is not optimistic about their character; he is confident about God’s. A drowning man held by a lifeguard is safe not because of how well he grips but because of how well he is gripped (John 10:27–28).

The hand that holds us. He never starts what he does not finish. He finished creation and rested. The Son finished the work the Father gave him and said from the cross, “It is finished”. Of all that the Father has given him he will lose nothing (John 6:39), and the hand that holds us bears the marks of what it cost him to reach us.

What it does not mean. Not that believers are passive: God works in us as we work out our salvation (2:12–13), which makes effort not pointless but hopeful. Nor that anyone who once prayed a prayer may live as he likes and be sure of heaven. A work of God shows itself in a changed and changing life.

What about people who seemed to be real Christians and then walked away? The honest answer has two parts. We cannot see hearts: some who seemed strong were never born again, and their leaving reveals it (1 John 2:19; Matthew 13:20–21). And some who wander are true believers in a terrible season, whom God will bring back, as he brought back Peter after his denial and David after his fall. We often cannot tell which is which until the end. So do not write anyone off, and do not pretend all is well: keep praying, keep loving, keep calling them home. The final judgment belongs to God, and so does the power to restore.

I feel I am going backwards. Has God stopped working in me? No. Growth is not a straight line, and it is often invisible from inside; seasons of dryness are often where God digs deeper foundations. Being troubled by your coldness is itself a sign of life: dead men do not grieve over their deadness. Go back to the means God uses: his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of believers. And rest on this verse: it does not say he will finish it if you feel it going well, but that he will finish it. Then do the next right thing, not to keep yourself saved, but because the one who keeps you is at work in you.

Where Christians differ: the perseverance of the saints. Many Christians in the Arminian tradition, who hold that God’s grace can be resisted, believe that a true believer can turn away and be finally lost. They are brothers and sisters who take Christ’s warnings with great seriousness, pointing to Hebrews 6:4–6 and to Paul’s own call to work out your own salvation with fear and trembling (2:12). This commentary’s view: Paul is confident that God will complete the work he began; salvation rests on God’s faithfulness, not our grip. The warnings are real and must be heeded, but the very next verse gives the reason the working out succeeds: it is God who works in you (2:13). True believers may stumble badly, but God will keep them to the end (John 6:39; 10:28–29; Romans 8:30). This is the perseverance of the saints, better called their preservation by God (the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, 17.1–2 in both). Those who fall away for good show that the work was never truly begun in them: they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19).

verseByVerse.quote: It is right for me to feel this way about you all, because I hold you in my heart, for you are all partakers with me of grace, both in my imprisonment and in the defense and confirmation of the gospel. For God is my witness, how I yearn for you all with the affection of Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has good reason to be so sure of them, for they share God’s grace with him even in his chains, and he longs for them with Christ’s own love.

It is right for me to feel this way. Not flattery but a justified confidence. The word for feel (phronein) is a favourite of this letter: to think, to have a settled mind, and it returns in the great command of 2:5, “Have this mind among yourselves”. He has thought about them and concluded that God is at work in them, and he holds them in his heart, carrying them with him into his cell.

Partakers with me of grace. Fellow sharers (synkoinōnoi), from the same root as the koinōnia of verse 5. They sent money and a man (2:25), so the ministry that money bought is theirs. The soldier who heard the gospel while guarding Paul heard it partly because a congregation in Macedonia had paid for Paul to be there.

Defence and confirmation. Both are courtroom words: apologia, the speech for the defence, and bebaiōsis, the legal establishing of a claim. Paul is on trial, and he tells a distant church that they stand in the dock with him. He counts even his imprisonment as part of the grace they share: the chains are not where grace ran out. So whoever prays for and funds a work they will never see is not on the sidelines of it.

With the affection of Christ Jesus. “Yearn” (epipotheō) is to ache to see. “Affection” translates splanchna, literally the inward organs: the ache in the stomach when you think of someone you love and cannot reach. The verb from the same word is used of Jesus, moved with compassion when he saw the crowds like sheep without a shepherd (Matthew 9:36). No one can verify an inward ache, so Paul calls God to witness.

Whose affection? Not merely Paul’s, felt strongly. What he feels for the Philippians is Christ’s own feeling for them, reaching them through a man in chains who cannot stop thinking about them. It is the love that took Christ to the cross, and whatever affection we feel for one another is a small stream from that great river.

What if I feel nothing for the people in my church? Do not pretend, and do not despair. You cannot produce Christ’s affection by trying to feel it, but it grows where the conditions are right. Pray for them by name, with thanks (vv. 3–4). Serve them practically, since feeling often follows action rather than preceding it. Spend time with them: Paul’s love was built over ten years of shared life and suffering. And ask Christ to love them through you; he is more willing to give his affection than you are to receive it.

Uncertain wording. In the Greek, “because I hold you in my heart” is an infinitive with two pronouns, either of which can be its subject, so it can also be read the other way round: “because you hold me in your heart”. Grammar alone cannot settle it, and both are true of a church that had sent one of its own on the long journey to look after him. The ESV’s reading is the more natural, since the sentence is about Paul’s feelings for them, and most translations follow it.

verseByVerse.quote: And it is my prayer that your love may abound more and more, with knowledge and all discernment, so that you may approve what is excellent, and so be pure and blameless for the day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prays that their love will overflow with knowledge and discernment, so that they choose what matters most and are ready for the day of Christ, full of the fruit only he can produce.

That your love may abound. Having given thanks, Paul asks: not that their circumstances would ease or the church grow, but that their love would grow, though he has just thanked God for it. The verb (perisseuō) is a flooding word: love overflowing its banks.

With knowledge and all discernment. An overflowing river without banks is a disaster, so Paul names the banks. Knowledge (epignōsis): settled knowledge, above all of God. Discernment (aisthēsis): trained senses, the moral sensitivity that knows what a situation needs. Love that abounds with these is no less warm; it is warm and can see. This church needed both: a generous congregation with a quarrel inside it (4:2), and teachers at the door whom Paul will warn against in the plainest terms (3:2, 18–19).

Two opposite failures. Most of us lean towards one. Love without discernment cannot say no, is taken in by every plausible teacher, enables what it should confront, and calls its softness kindness. Discernment without love is never taken in, can spot an error at fifty paces, and has a cold and shrinking heart. The first is sentimentality; the second is not far from cruelty. Paul asks for a love grown enough to know what it is doing.

Approve what is excellent. To test and, having tested, approve, as metal is assayed (dokimazō). What is excellent (ta diapheronta) means the things that differ, the things that really matter. The hardest choices are rarely between good and evil, but between good and best, two legitimate claims on the same evening. Choosing well there needs love with its senses trained.

Pure and blameless. Then the goal: to be ready for the day of Christ named in verse 6. “Pure” (eilikrinēs) may come from holding a thing up to the sunlight to test it: a pure life shows no hidden flaws or mixed motives when the light shines through. “Blameless” (aproskopos) means without stumbling, and can also mean not causing others to stumble; both fit.

The fruit of righteousness. Then the source, which rescues the prayer from being a to-do list: fruit that comes through him, as sap comes through a branch that has no life of its own. “As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me” (John 15:4). And it is “to the glory and praise of God”: Paul asks God to do this in them, so the glory is his.

Held up to the light. On the day of Christ the light will get behind every life, and the people of Jesus will be held up to it and found pure. Not one of them will owe it to himself. The love that grew in them was his love, the righteousness that covers them his own, and when the harvest is gathered, every voice will say whose work it was.

Is this fruit of righteousness the same as being justified? Not quite, but the two are joined. Here Paul means the righteous life that grows in a believer: love, honesty, purity, good works. In chapter 3 he speaks of the righteousness from God that depends on faith (3:9), Christ’s perfect righteousness counted to us when we believe. That is the root; this is the fruit. We are not accepted because of the fruit; we bear fruit because we have been accepted and joined to Christ.

How does my love actually grow in knowledge and discernment? By being soaked in God’s word, which trains the senses to distinguish good from evil (Hebrews 5:14): read it asking what it shows you about loving God and people. Watch how mature Christians handle hard situations. Practise: facing a decision, ask not only whether it is allowed but what would be most loving and most for Christ’s glory. Discernment grows like a muscle, by use and slowly. And pray this prayer, phrase by phrase, for someone you love, instead of praying that their week would go smoothly, and notice how different a thing you are asking for.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–26 — The Chains, the Rivals, and the Choice
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul’s chains, his rivals and even the prospect of death all serve one end: that Christ is made known and honoured. His imprisonment has carried the gospel into the imperial guard and made other believers bold (vv. 12–14). Even rivals who preach Christ to wound him are spreading the message, so he rejoices (vv. 15–18). Sure of the outcome through their prayers and the Spirit, he wants only that Christ be honoured in his body, by life or by death, for to live is Christ and to die is gain (vv. 19–21). Torn between departing to be with Christ and staying, he expects to remain for their progress and joy in the faith (vv. 22–26).
verseByVerse.theology:
Providence: The Chains Were Not a Setback

What Paul reports here is Romans 8:28 lived out: God working all things together for good. God’s providence is not the salvaging of a situation that got away from him but his active government of all things, hostile human choices included, toward his own saving purposes. Paul knew he had been stationed, not merely detained (see the note on vv. 15–17).

The same truth governs his response to the rival preachers (see the note on v. 18).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul writes as a prisoner whose usefulness looked finished, to a church funding a mission that appeared to have stalled, and reports what God has in fact done (vv. 12–14).

Now: For the believer whose life has been derailed, verse 12 is an invitation, not a demand (see the note on vv. 12–13).

verseByVerse.quote: I want you to know, brothers, that what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel, so that it has become known throughout the whole imperial guard and to all the rest that my imprisonment is for Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s imprisonment has not stopped the gospel but carried it forward, right into the emperor’s own guard. The news the Philippians dreaded has turned out to be good news.

What has happened to me. Paul turns to what they must have been agonising over: their apostle is in chains, and from every ordinary angle the mission has stalled. (“Brothers” includes the sisters of the church, Lydia among them.)

To advance the gospel. “Advance” is forward movement (prokopē), sometimes pictured as pioneers cutting a road ahead of an army. His imprisonment is not a roadblock but roadworks: the chains are not what happened instead of the gospel’s progress but the instrument of it.

The whole imperial guard. Most likely the Praetorian Guard, the emperor’s elite household troops (see the end of this note). Paul lived with a soldier assigned to him (Acts 28:16, 20), presumably relieved shift by shift: some of the empire’s most trusted soldiers, one after another, chained beside a prisoner who could not stop talking about Christ. The Roman state had accidentally built Paul a captive congregation and paid for the guards. By the end of the letter he sends greetings from believers in Caesar’s household (4:22).

For Christ. What became known was not only the message but the reason: this man was in custody not for sedition or fraud, but for a Galilean he claimed was alive.

The bound Lord. Christ had worn chains first. Soldiers seized Jesus in the garden, bound him and led him from court to court (John 18:12–13, 24), and to every onlooker his mission had ended. Yet the cross that looked like the gospel’s defeat was its accomplishment. The word advances through a bound servant because it first advanced through a bound Saviour. The preacher may be bound, but the word of God is not bound (2 Timothy 2:9).

Said carefully. “God will use it” can be a cruel thing to say too early. Paul is not offering optimism that bad things turn out fine, but reporting what God has done, with soldiers to show for it. The man whose career was ended by illness, or whose ministry closed when the church split, need not feel that his loss is a gain; he is invited to consider that the God who turned a prison into a pulpit is not out of options. Paul wrote verse 12 from the far side of the disappointment; most of us are asked to trust it from the near side.

In everyday life. Name the circumstance you would most like to change: the job, the illness, the limitation. Then ask who is chained to you in it: the colleague on your shift, the nurse, the family member who sees you every day. They are watching how a Christian bears what he did not choose; make sure they know why.

Does God cause my hard circumstances, or only use them? Scripture holds two things together. God is not the author of sin: the men who arrested Paul were responsible for what they did. Yet nothing happens outside God’s rule, and he governs even wicked acts for his good purposes, as Joseph told his brothers: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). So it was supremely at the cross (Acts 2:23). You need not blame God for evil, nor fear that evil has escaped him. Your hardship is not random or wasted; it is held in a Father’s hand.

Is it wrong to pray to get out of my situation? No. Paul himself hoped to be released (vv. 19, 25), and Jesus prayed that the cup might pass from him. Pray honestly for relief, and pray also that while you are there Christ will be made known through you. The soldiers chained to Paul needed not his release but his faithfulness where he was.

Uncertain wording. The Greek says simply “the whole praetorium”, which can mean a place, a governor’s headquarters (Herod’s praetorium in Caesarea, Acts 23:35), or people, the Praetorian Guard. “And to all the rest” suggests people, hence the ESV’s “imperial guard”, and if Paul wrote from Rome (see the introduction) the emperor’s guard is the natural sense. Either way, those who held Paul knew why he was there.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “imperial guard” is literally “the whole praetorium” — the Roman soldiers guarding him, or the governor’s headquarters.

verseByVerse.quote: And most of the brothers, having become confident in the Lord by my imprisonment, are much more bold to speak the word without fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s chains have made most of the believers around him braver, not more cautious. Seeing what the Lord was doing through a prisoner, they trusted him more and spoke the word without fear.

Confident in the Lord. The second advance is quieter than the first and, in the long run, larger. You would expect the opposite: when the leader is arrested, the sensible move is to lower your voice and wait for the weather to change. Their confidence rests in the Lord, not in Paul, nor in a hope that the authorities were bluffing; his chains proved not that the risk was small but that the gospel was worth it.

Most of the brothers. Most, not all. Some in Rome went quiet, and Paul says so without naming or scolding them: his sentence leaves room for the believer who has gone quiet under pressure, without excusing him.

Without fear. “Bold” is to dare (tolmaō), and “without fear” (aphobōs) stands at the end of the sentence like a flag. These were not people who felt no fear, but people who spoke anyway, where it cost something.

They had been with Jesus. Paul’s chains showed not how strong he was but how faithful his Lord is. The risen Christ had promised to be with his witnesses always (Matthew 28:20), and a prisoner full of joy was that promise kept in public. When the council saw the boldness of Peter and John, it recognised that they had been with Jesus (Acts 4:13). Such courage is not a temperament but what happens to ordinary people who are sure that Christ stands beside them.

Faithfulness multiplies. One person willing to bear the loss of a job, a friendship or standing in the family quietly makes everyone watching a little braver. Nobody in Rome had planned it. The believer paying a price unseen may be doing more for those around him than he will learn in this life. Courage is contagious; so, sadly, is cowardice.

What it does not mean. Not that every Christian is called to be reckless or to court arrest. Boldness to speak the word is not harshness; the New Testament joins it to gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15).

I have gone quiet about my faith at work. What do I do? Begin with honesty before God: confess the fear without excusing it, and remember that Peter, who denied Christ three times, became the boldest preacher in Jerusalem. Then take one small step: answer truthfully next time someone asks what you did at the weekend; say you will pray for a struggling colleague, and do it. Ask God for boldness, as the first church did (Acts 4:29), and let your confidence rest in the Lord, not in your own nerve. Courage usually grows by use.

verseByVerse.quote: Some indeed preach Christ from envy and rivalry, but others from good will. The latter do it out of love, knowing that I am put here for the defense of the gospel. The former proclaim Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely but thinking to afflict me in my imprisonment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some preach Christ out of love for Paul, others out of envy, hoping to hurt him; Paul names both honestly and is not shaken, because he knows where God has put him.

Envy and rivalry. A genuinely ugly detail, and Paul does not soften it. Some preachers in Rome were jealous of him and saw his imprisonment as their chance to gain influence; they preached Christ to hurt him. Envy (phthonos) is resentment at another’s good; rivalry (eris) is strife, the spirit that must win.

Others from good will. In a passage about envy it is easy to remember only the rivals. Paul had friends in Rome who preached because they loved him and loved Christ. Most churches contain both sorts, and a Christian wounded by the first kind can end up unable to see the second.

I am put here. To be laid, set, appointed (keimai): what you say of a sentry given a post, or a stone set in a foundation. Paul does not regard himself as a man who was arrested, but as a man who was posted.

Selfish ambition. Party spirit, self-promotion (eritheia): a rare word before Paul, used by Aristotle of men seeking public office for what they could get out of it. It returns in 2:3, where the Philippians are to do nothing from it: Paul is showing them, in real life, the disease he is about to warn them against. Their motives were wrong, but their message was right.

Thinking to afflict me. Literally to raise up affliction for him: to add pressure to a man already in chains, calculating that his rivals’ success would grieve and perhaps sour him. Most men would have been soured. Paul was not.

Handed over out of envy. Envy met the Lord before it met his apostle. Pilate perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed Jesus over (Mark 15:10), and God used their envy to accomplish the salvation of the world. Envy could not stop the Master’s work, and it will not stop the servant’s. For all their spite, the only weapon the rivals could find against Paul was to preach Christ.

A sentry, not an unlucky prisoner. If Paul is an unlucky prisoner, his rivals are getting away with something and his life has been interrupted. If he is a posted sentry, nothing has miscarried: he is where his Commander stationed him, holding ground he did not choose. Everyone somewhere he did not choose, a job, a marriage, a sickbed, a town, must decide which describes his life: the facts are the same, but the life looks completely different. Christ is the Commander who posts his servants, and nowhere is outside his map. So say it over the place you did not choose: not stranded, not forgotten, not interrupted. Posted.

Who were these rival preachers? Paul does not name them, and we do not know. They preached the true gospel, since Paul rejoices in their message (v. 18), but resented his prominence, perhaps because they had led the Roman churches before he arrived, or because his imprisonment seemed to them a disgrace. They were not false teachers, and that makes the passage more searching: orthodox, gifted, busy Christian workers can be driven by envy, and not notice.

How do I know whether my own service is driven by rivalry? Ask uncomfortable questions. How do I feel when another’s ministry flourishes more than mine? Am I glad when good work is done that no one will connect with me? Do I find it hard to praise a fellow worker in his absence? Would I keep serving if nobody noticed? If the answers sting, do not despair. Confess it, ask God to purify your heart, and make a habit of praying by name for the success of those you feel rivalry towards (compare vv. 3–5).

Textual note. The KJV and NKJV give verses 16 and 17 in the opposite order, following later manuscripts; the earliest have the order of most modern Bibles, and the sense is unchanged.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Only that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed, and in that I rejoice. Yes, and I will rejoice,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever the preachers’ motives, Christ is being proclaimed, and that is enough to make Paul glad now and to keep him glad.

What then? A shrug you can hear: a man setting an injury down. He has just described people trying to wound him; now he weighs it, and finds it does not weigh much.

In pretence or in truth. “Pretence” (prophasis) is a pretext, a show covering the real motive. Motives matter: he has just called theirs envy and selfish ambition (compare 2:3). Nor is any message preached under Christ’s name acceptable: the man who wrote Galatians 1:8–9 would call down a curse on a preacher whose content was false. The rivals were preaching the true gospel with rotten hearts, and that case is the only one Paul addresses.

The power is in the message. A true gospel preached from a bad motive is still a true gospel, and its hearers can still be saved by it. God is not so particular that he would let a soul perish rather than use a flawed servant, which is a mercy, since he has never had any other kind to use. We have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us (2 Corinthians 4:7).

And in that I rejoice. The rivals’ strategy depended on his caring more about his own standing than about Christ’s, and it failed for the reason he gives three verses later: to him, to live is Christ. Attack such a man by advancing Christ, and you have handed him a present. They aimed at his pride, and it was no longer there to hit.

Yes, and I will rejoice. Present tense, then future. He rejoices now, in a cell, over preachers who despise him, and commits to going on rejoicing before he knows his verdict. That second clause is a decision, not a feeling. Joy in this letter is something Paul chooses and then commands (3:1; 4:4), which is possible only because its reason lies outside him, in Christ.

What it does not mean. Not that we should be indifferent to the character of preachers and leaders. Elders must be above reproach (1 Timothy 3:2), and a church must deal with leaders whose lives deny their message. Paul is not lowering the standard; he is refusing to let his wounded feelings decide whether he rejoices that Christ is known.

How can I rejoice when others get the credit or outshine me? By changing what you rejoice in. If your joy is in your own usefulness, every success of another is a small loss; if it is in Christ being known, every success of another is your gain too. John the Baptist showed the way when his disciples complained that everyone was going to Jesus: he must increase, but I must decrease (John 3:30). Thank God aloud for others’ fruitfulness, especially those who have hurt you; refuse to talk down another’s ministry; and remember that every faithful labour will be rewarded by the only judge whose opinion matters (1 Corinthians 3:8).

verseByVerse.quote: for I know that through your prayers and the help of the Spirit of Jesus Christ this will turn out for my deliverance,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is sure that, through the church’s prayers and the Spirit’s full supply, all this will end in his vindication before God, whatever the Roman court decides.

This will turn out for my deliverance. The words are a quotation, word for word, from the Greek Old Testament at Job 13:16. Job says them when his friends have finished explaining that his suffering proves his guilt, and he turns to argue his case with God, hoping not for his cattle back but for a hearing. Paul, with his own accusers circling, makes the sentence his, joining the line of the righteous sufferer whom God proves right, not by sparing him affliction but by bringing him through it. Deliverance (sōtēria) is the ordinary New Testament word for salvation. Paul does not chiefly mean release, since the next verse reckons with life or death; he means that this will end in his standing before God unashamed.

Through your prayers and the help of the Spirit. The Greek joins the two so closely that they read as one supply line. “Help” is epichorēgia, generous, full supply: the Spirit does not send occasional relief but supplies all a believer needs to endure, and he is the Spirit of Jesus Christ, sent by the Son to his people (Galatians 4:6). The Philippians pray in Macedonia; the Spirit supplies in Rome; Paul treats them as one movement. That is a high view of ordinary intercession: when you pray for a Christian in a hard place, you are inside the supply line, and Paul says plainly that he was counting on it.

The vindicated Sufferer. Paul can borrow Job’s sentence because the great righteous Sufferer has already been vindicated, shown by God to be in the right. Jesus was condemned by every court that heard him, and on the third day God reversed the verdict: he was declared to be the Son of God in power by his resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:4). Paul’s hope of standing unashamed rests not on how well he speaks before Caesar but on the one who stood in the dock for him and was raised.

If God is sovereign, do my prayers actually change anything? Yes, because God has ordained the means as well as the ends, and prayer is one of his chosen means. Paul expected God to work through their prayers, not apart from them. God needs no informing and is not persuaded against his will; but he has bound himself to answer his children, and delights to draw us into his work. You have not, because you ask not (James 4:2). Sovereignty is not a reason to stop praying but the reason prayer is not wasted: the one you are speaking to can actually do it.

In everyday life. Choose one Christian in a hard place and pray for them by name every day this week, not only for relief but for what Paul wanted: that they would not be ashamed, and that Christ would be honoured in them. Tell them you are praying.

verseByVerse.quote: as it is my eager expectation and hope that I will not be at all ashamed, but that with full courage now as always Christ will be honored in my body, whether by life or by death. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s one hope is that Christ will be shown to be great in his body, whether he lives or dies, because Christ is his whole life and death can only bring him more of Christ.

Eager expectation. One word, often pictured as craning forward with outstretched neck (apokaradokia), used of the whole creation waiting for the revealing of the sons of God (Romans 8:19). Paul is not merely enduring; he is leaning forward in hope.

Not at all ashamed. The fear is not execution. It is that under pressure he might crack, deny, hedge or go quiet, and so bring dishonour on the name.

Honoured in my body. “Honoured” is to magnify (megalynō): not as a microscope makes small things look bigger than they are, but as a telescope makes things unimaginably great and far away look as great as they really are. A life can do that for Christ. And it happens in this physical, chained, ageing body, the only place any of us honours Christ: in how we speak to our family, handle a temptation or bear pain.

For to me to live is Christ. Nine words in Greek. Weigh what he did not write: not “Christ is important to me”, nor “Christ is the centre of my life”, which still leaves a life with Christ installed in the middle of it. Living is Christ. Take him out of the sentence and nothing is left: living means knowing him, serving him, loving him, being loved by him. Fill in the blank honestly and the verse becomes a test of the heart. For to me to live is ____, and whatever word arrives unbidden is the thing whose loss would end you. Look at where your thoughts go when they are free, where your money goes, what makes you anxious.

And to die is gain. If living is Christ, dying cannot be loss; it can only be more of what living was already about: being with him (v. 23). Death does not interrupt such a life; it brings it home. Put anything else in the blank, family, work, health, reputation, and death is what it appears to be at every graveside: the end of the only thing you had. The second half of the verse is not a brave saying added on. It follows from the first as surely as a sum.

The gain is him. Christ is the only one both worth living for and worth dying for: the one thing not lost at the grave but gained there, magnified in weak and chained and dying bodies, because his power is made perfect in weakness. To live is Christ; to die is gain; and the gain is him.

Death as a technical problem. Our age has a new answer to death: postpone it. The historian Yuval Noah Harari argued in Homo Deus (2016) that, having largely tamed famine, plague and war, humanity would turn next to overcoming death itself, as a technical problem awaiting a technical solution. Some of the richest people alive spend fortunes on that hope, and the rest of us track our sleep and steps in a smaller version of it. Healthy years are a good gift, and medicine is a mercy. But a longer life still has to be about something, and it still ends. Paul, facing possible execution, neither clutches at extra years nor resigns himself to the void. He has found the one thing death cannot take and can only bring nearer, and that rests not on a better technique but on a Person who went through death and came out the other side (see the note on 1 Corinthians 15:12–19).

What it does not mean. Not that Paul wished to die or despised this life; both are good, because Christ is in both. Nor that a Christian should lose interest in his family, his work or the good gifts of creation. Christ is not in competition with them. A life that is Christ loves its wife more, works more honestly and enjoys a meal more gratefully, because it receives everything from his hand and does everything for him.

I cannot honestly say that to live is Christ. What then? Most Christians cannot say it as fully as Paul, and the honesty is a good beginning; he wrote it after nearly thirty years of walking with Christ and suffering for him. Do not try to work up a feeling; ask God to make it true, and give Christ more of your attention: in his word, where you see his glory; in prayer; at the Lord’s Supper. We become like what we behold (2 Corinthians 3:18). Often the remedy is not to love the good gift in the blank less, but to love the Giver more, so that the gift takes its proper place.

verseByVerse.quote: If I am to live in the flesh, that means fruitful labor for me. Yet which I shall choose I cannot tell. I am hard pressed between the two. My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is torn between departing to be with Christ, which is far better, and staying to serve the church, which they need, and love for them tips the balance.

Fruitful labour. An apostle unable to decide whether he would rather live or be executed. Living means more gospel fruit: churches strengthened, people brought to Christ, letters like this one.

Which I shall choose I cannot tell. Not that the verdict is his to decide, but that he cannot say which he would prefer, because both are good. Hard pressed (synechomai) means squeezed from both sides.

To depart. “Depart” (analyō) is used of untying a ship from the quay, striking a tent, unyoking an animal after the day’s work, loosing a prisoner from his chains. Each is a release, and each implies somewhere to go. That is Paul’s word for dying: not extinction but casting off. Waiting for execution years later, he used the noun: the time of my departure has come (2 Timothy 4:6).

Far better. A window onto what happens when a believer dies: Paul expects to be with Christ, immediately, consciously, and better. Literally “much more better”: one word is not enough for him. Compare the promise from the cross, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43), and at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Christ has prayed that those the Father gave him may be with him where he is, to see his glory (John 17:24), and that prayer is answered every time a Christian dies.

Far better, not yet best. To be with Christ at death is far better than this life, but not yet the best: the best is the resurrection of the body when he appears, which Paul comes to at 3:20–21. The Christian dead are not kept waiting outside, for they are with Christ; but they are still waiting for the resurrection.

More necessary on your account. Here the passage becomes searching. Having said that departing is far better, Paul concludes that he will stay: the tie-breaker is not his preference but their need. He wants the better thing and chooses the useful one. Every week brings most of us a small version of the same choice, the rest you have earned or the person who needs you tonight, and Paul shows which way a man leans when Christ has become his life.

Is it wrong for a Christian to long to die? Paul longed to be with Christ, and so may every believer, especially in suffering. But look at what he did with the longing. He did not act on it; he left the timing to God and gave himself to the people who needed him (vv. 24–25). Wanting heaven is faith; taking one’s own life is not, because our times are in God’s hand (Psalm 31:15). So this passage does not make suicide acceptable. Anyone whose longing for death has become a plan should get help today, from a doctor or a crisis line (emergency services if the danger is immediate), and tell a pastor and a friend, and hear what Paul concluded: to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account. You are needed here. And if you have lost a believer to suicide, this verse is not a verdict on the one you loved: nothing in all creation can separate God’s people from his love in Christ (Romans 8:38–39).

If death is gain, is it wrong to grieve when a Christian dies? No. Jesus wept at the grave of Lazarus (John 11:35), knowing he was about to raise him, and Paul speaks of the sorrow he would have had if Epaphroditus had died (2:27). Death is still an enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26), and parting hurts; what changes is the kind of grief: we grieve, but not as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). The one who died in Christ has gained; we have lost, for a while. So weep, and let others weep with you, holding on to this: the one you miss is with Christ, far better off, and you will see them again.

Do believers who have died know what is happening on earth? Scripture does not say that they watch over us, and we should not build on guesses; what it says is enough: they are with Christ, conscious, at rest and far better off (Revelation 14:13). We are not to pray to them or try to contact them (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). Our communion with them is through the one Lord we share: whenever you draw near to Christ, you are near to the one in whose presence they now are.

Where Christians differ: the intermediate state. Where are believers between death and the resurrection? Some Christians, Seventh-day Adventists among them, believe the dead sleep unconsciously until then, since Scripture often calls death sleep; but that word describes how death looks from this side, not the state of the soul. Roman Catholic teaching adds purgatory, a place of further cleansing after death. This commentary’s view: Paul says to depart is to be with Christ, and far better; he could not weigh unconscious nothing against fruitful labour and call it far better. Believers who die go immediately into Christ’s conscious presence, where they await the resurrection of the body (2 Corinthians 5:8; Luke 23:43; the Westminster Confession 32.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1). Nor is there any purgatory in between: Paul expects to go straight to Christ, and the blood of Christ has already cleansed those who are his from all sin.

verseByVerse.quote: Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and continue with you all, for your progress and joy in the faith, so that in me you may have ample cause to glory in Christ Jesus, because of my coming to you again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul expects to stay alive for the church’s sake, so that they may grow and rejoice in the faith, and overflow with boasting in Christ when he comes back to them.

I know that I will remain. Since his continuing is what the churches need, Paul expects to be given it. He is not claiming a revelation about the trial; in 2:17 he still reckons with being poured out as a drink offering. He trusts that God cares about the churches’ needs at least as much as he does. And he probably was released: the letters to Timothy and Titus suggest he travelled again before a second imprisonment and his death (1 Timothy 1:3; 2 Timothy 4:6).

Your progress and joy in the faith. “Progress” is the word (prokopē) used of the gospel advancing through his chains (1:12); now it is the Philippians who are to advance. That is a striking measure of a pastor’s ambition: not their comfort or their numbers, but their movement forward, and their gladness in it. Joy is not a temperament for the sunnier sort of Christian but something a congregation can make progress in.

Ample cause to glory in Christ Jesus. “To glory” is to boast with joy. Paul imagines walking through the gate at Philippi and the church overflowing with gladness, and he is careful to say where it is to go: not to him, but through him to Christ.

Heaven postponed for others. Paul makes on a small scale the choice the next chapter describes on the grandest. The Son had the better place by right, the form of God and the Father’s glory, and he did not count it a thing to be grasped, but came down for people who needed him (2:6–7). Paul, offered what is far better, stays for the Philippians’ progress. He is not a second saviour and can give them nothing Christ has not given. But a man who has been loved like that begins to love like that, and it is the mind of Christ in Paul that weighs a congregation’s joy against his own heaven and chooses the congregation.

He did not make them feel like the obstacle. After saying he would rather be with Christ, a lesser man would have left the church feeling like the reason he was stuck here. Paul says he is glad to be convinced that he will stay; his longing for glory never becomes a rebuke to the people who still need him.

How can I know what God will do in my situation? Usually not in detail, and Scripture does not promise that you will know. You can know what Paul knew: that God works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28), that he will complete his work in you (v. 6), and that Christ will be honoured whether by life or by death. Reason from those truths, plan humbly, say if the Lord wills (James 4:15), and leave the rest with him. Paul’s confidence was really confidence in God’s goodness, and that is open to every believer.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Whatever happens to Paul, the Philippians are to live as citizens of heaven, and that means standing together, unafraid. Their manner of life is to match the gospel, one in spirit and mind, striving side by side for the faith (v. 27). Their calm before opponents is God’s sign of their salvation and of their opponents’ ruin (v. 28), for suffering for Christ, like believing in him, is a gift of grace, and in it they share Paul’s own contest (vv. 29–30).
verseByVerse.theology:
Suffering as a Gift of Grace

Suffering for Christ is granted (v. 29), given by grace as faith is given (see the note on vv. 29–30). In this present age it is a normal part of the Christian life, not an exception: through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In a garrison colony where loyalty to the emperor was ordinary civic decency, confessing another Lord looked like disloyalty to the city (see the note on v. 27).

Now: Being opposed does not prove you are right; the calm God gives under opposition for the gospel does (see the note on v. 28).

verseByVerse.quote: Only let your manner of life be worthy of the gospel of Christ, so that whether I come and see you or am absent, I may hear of you that you are standing firm in one spirit, with one mind striving side by side for the faith of the gospel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever happens to Paul, the Philippians are to live as citizens of heaven in a way that matches the gospel, standing together as one. This single command is the one the rest of the letter unpacks.

Let your manner of life be worthy of the gospel. With “only”, Paul turns from his situation to theirs. The verb, politeuesthe, is, from polis, city: to live as a citizen of a commonwealth. Paul usually says “walk”; here he chooses a citizen’s word.

A colony of heaven. Philippi was where this would land hardest: a Roman colony, a little Rome on Macedonian soil whose people held Roman citizenship (see the introduction): Roman law, Latin in the forum, a city answering to a capital some eight hundred miles away, whose business was to represent it accurately on this frontier. So Paul says: be citizens, worthy of the gospel. There is a capital, and it is not Rome; there is a Lord, and he is not Caesar. You are the outpost. He will make the point explicit at 3:20, “But our citizenship is in heaven”, but he plants it here in a single verb.

Worthy does not mean earning. A colonist does not earn his citizenship by good behaviour; he already has it, and lives in a way that matches it. Grace first, then a life that fits the grace. Worthy (axiōs) is a word from weighing: a life that balances the gospel it claims, as one pan of a scale balances the other, so that onlookers are not misled about the gospel. No colonist’s life matches it perfectly, and the citizenship never rested on that: it rests on Christ, whose perfect obedience is counted as ours (3:9; Romans 5:19), so a failure sends us back to him, not out of the city.

Whether I come and see you or am absent. The test of a church is what it is like when the apostle is not in the room. Conduct worthy of the gospel is not a performance for visiting authority; it is what the colony is like on an ordinary Tuesday, with the capital a long way off. Every faithful congregation holding the line on an ordinary week is a small embassy of the city that will last when Rome and every other empire is dust.

Standing firm in one spirit. “Standing firm” (stēkō) is what a battle line does when it holds. “In one spirit” may mean one shared spirit among them, or the one Holy Spirit who unites them (compare 2:1); the two belong together, because the one Spirit makes them one.

With one mind striving side by side. “With one mind” is literally with one soul; “striving side by side” is synathleō, competing together as a team. Both pictures require other people: a man alone is not a line. They strive for the faith of the gospel, believed and defended, and this is the answer, planted early, to the quarrel Paul will name in 4:2.

What does unity look like when Christians in the same church disagree? First, distinguish. On the gospel itself there must be one mind, and Paul will not compromise it; on many other matters believers may differ in conscience (Romans 14:1–5). Then keep the main thing in view: you are side by side against a common opponent, not face to face against each other. Speak to the person, not about them (Matthew 18:15). Assume the best motives you honestly can. Be quick to apologise for your share. And keep turning up, serving and praying together, because the line holds when people stand next to each other, not when they agree about everything.

In everyday life. Ask what someone watching your life this week would conclude about the capital you belong to. Then ask whether there is anyone at church you have stopped standing beside. The Spirit who joined you to them is the strength to stand there again: a conversation, an apology, an invitation, a shared task.
verseByVerse.note: The word for “manner of life” means living as a citizen — fitting for a Roman colony proud of its status.

verseByVerse.quote: and not frightened in anything by your opponents. This is a clear sign to them of their destruction, but of your salvation, and that from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not let your opponents stampede you: a church that holds its ground calmly is God’s own evidence that they are losing and you are saved.

Not frightened in anything. Frightened is a word used of horses (ptyromenoi): the sudden shying of an animal that has caught a movement in the hedge, the bolt, the panic that runs through a line and breaks it. The Philippians faced opposition in a city fiercely loyal to Caesar, where Paul and Silas had been charged with advocating customs unlawful for Romans (Acts 16:21).

Fear refused the reins. Paul does not forbid feeling fear. The word describes the bolting, not the pulse rate, so a believer who is afraid and stays put has obeyed this verse completely. Courage in Scripture is almost never the absence of fear; it is fear refused the reins. And ask what the fear is made of. Much of our dread of opponents is really a longing for their approval: we are less afraid of being hurt than of being thought foolish. The fear of the Lord is the cure for the fear of man (Proverbs 29:25; Matthew 10:28): once his verdict is the one that matters, theirs loses its grip.

A clear sign to them. A proof (endeixis), a law-court word: the steadiness of a frightened little church is submitted as evidence, and it says two things. To the persecutors it is the first indication that they are fighting a losing battle against God, because people do not stand like that over nothing. To the church it confirms that they are truly God’s, “and that from God”: the courage is his gift. Self-generated courage would prove only that they were brave that week; God-given courage is real evidence.

A battle already decided. Why should a small church’s steadiness tell its persecutors anything about their end? Because at the cross God disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them in him (Colossians 2:15). The church does not hold its ground in order to win. It holds its ground because Christ has won, and its calm is a small, visible echo of his empty tomb.

What it does not mean. Not that being disliked proves you are right. Plenty of people are opposed because they are obnoxious, and this verse is no shelter for them; let none of you suffer as a wrongdoer, Peter says (1 Peter 4:15). Paul means opposition incurred for the gospel, met without panic. It is the composure, not the conflict, that is the evidence.

Who are my opponents, if I am not being persecuted? In the West opposition is often quieter than in Philippi, but real: mockery at work or school, family members who resent your faith, pressure to keep silent about what Scripture teaches, the threat of losing a job or a friendship. Elsewhere believers face prison and death, and you should pray for them. Remember too that the real enemy is not people; we do not wrestle against flesh and blood (Ephesians 6:12). Those who oppose you are to be won, not crushed, and your steady, gentle courage may be the evidence God uses to bring them to himself, as he did with a jailer in Philippi.

What if I have already panicked and run? Then you stand where Peter stood after the rooster crowed. He bolted, and Jesus restored him, asked him three times whether he loved him, and sent him back to feed the sheep (John 21:15–19). Within weeks he stood before the council that had condemned his Lord, astonishing them with his boldness. Confess your failure to God, and to others if they were affected. Then go back to your place in the line. Your courage was never meant to come from you anyway; it is from God.

verseByVerse.quote: For it has been granted to you that for the sake of Christ you should not only believe in him but also suffer for his sake, engaged in the same conflict that you saw I had and now hear that I still have.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believing in Christ and suffering for him are both gifts of God’s grace, and in their suffering the Philippians share Paul’s own contest. Their hardship is not a sign that God has left them.

It has been granted to you. Given as a gift: the little word that carries this verse (echaristhē) comes from charis, grace. Under that one word Paul sets two things side by side: to believe in Christ, and to suffer for his sake.

Not only believe in him. Even faith is not the one thing we contribute to our salvation but a gift God grants (Ephesians 2:8; Acts 13:48). The Spirit gives new birth, making alive someone who was dead towards God, so that he now sees Christ as glorious and gladly trusts him (John 3:3–8; Ephesians 2:4–5). In Philippi itself the first convert believed because the Lord opened her heart (Acts 16:14).

But also suffer for his sake. Paul writes not to settle a debate about the will but to steady a frightened church (v. 28), and it is this second gift he wants them to feel. Suffering for Christ is not a sign that grace has run out but a grace in its own right, a share in his sufferings given to those who truly belong to him. The apostles left the council “rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name” (Acts 5:41). So the Philippians were to read their hardship not as God’s abandonment but as real fellowship with their Lord (1 Peter 4:13).

The same conflict that you saw I had. They had watched it: Paul and Silas dragged into the marketplace, stripped, beaten with rods and thrown into the inner prison, then praying and singing hymns to God at midnight (Acts 16:19–25). “Conflict” is agōn, the contest in the arena where they strive side by side (v. 27). One contest, and Paul and this church are in it together.

The fellowship of the cross. To be joined to a crucified and risen Lord is to share both his death and his resurrection (3:10); you cannot take the one and refuse the other. A faith that expects to be spared all hardship has misread the very gift it was given. Suffering for his sake is neither wasted nor a punishment; it is the fellowship of the cross, and one day it opens into the fellowship of the glory (Romans 8:17).

Chains at midnight, hymns in the dark. He gives us to believe in him, and then the honour of sharing his road. He went first into the arena and bore the full weight of the cross alone, so that no suffering of his people would ever be a sign of his anger. The night of beating and singing in Philippi is the pattern of the whole Christian life: chains at midnight, hymns in the dark, and a door that God himself opens.

What it does not mean. Not that suffering is to be sought out: Paul never went looking for a beating, and he left Philippi when the magistrates asked him to. Nor that every hardship a Christian faces is suffering for Christ. Some suffering we bring on ourselves by folly or sin, and that is to be repented of, not celebrated.

Is my illness or bereavement suffering for Christ? Strictly, suffering for his sake is what comes on you because you belong to him and confess him: mockery, loss, opposition, persecution. Illness, grief and the ordinary troubles of a fallen world are not that in the same sense, but they are not outside his care. For those who love God, all things work together for good (Romans 8:28): borne trusting him, they too shape you into his Son’s likeness, and he is with you in them. In no kind of suffering is a believer alone or without purpose.

How can suffering be a gift when it hurts so much? The gift is not the pain itself but what God gives through it and with it: closer fellowship with Christ, who suffered first; proof that your faith is real; a share in his work; and a weight of glory beyond all comparison with the suffering (2 Corinthians 4:17; Romans 8:18). Paul’s chains hurt, yet they served to advance the gospel (1:12). You need not pretend to feel grateful in the moment. But you may ask God to help you see the hand that gives it, and trust that he gives his children nothing that is not, in the end, for their good.

Where Christians differ: is faith a gift? Many Christians, especially in the Arminian tradition, believe that God’s grace enables everyone to believe and that faith is our free response, the one thing we bring to God; they too prize grace and love the Saviour. This commentary’s view: Paul says believing in Christ was granted, given by grace. Faith is our act, but it is God’s gift, produced by the Spirit in regeneration (Ephesians 2:8–9; John 6:44, 65), so even faith gives no ground for boasting.
