This is what Reformed confessions call effectual calling, God’s inward call that actually brings a sinner to Christ: God gives the faith he requires (the Westminster Confession 10.1 and 14.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.1 and 14.1). It does not mean God forces people to believe. He changes the heart so that they gladly believe.
verseByVerse.note: Paul and Silas had been beaten and jailed at Philippi.

Yet which I shall choose I cannot tell.<sup>23</sup>I am hard pressed between the two. My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better.<sup>24</sup>But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account.<sup>25</sup>Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and continue with you all, for your progress and joy in the faith,<sup>26</sup>so that in me you may have ample cause to glory in Christ Jesus, because of my coming to you again.<sup>27</sup>Only let your manner of life be worthy of the gospel of Christ, so that whether I come and see you or am absent, I may hear of you that you are standing firm in one spirit, with one mind striving side by side for the faith of the gospel,<sup>28</sup>and not frightened in anything by your opponents. This is a clear sign to them of their destruction, but of your salvation, and that from God.<sup>29</sup>For it has been granted to you that for the sake of Christ you should not only believe in him but also suffer for his sake,<sup>30</sup>engaged in the same conflict that you saw I had and now hear that I still have.

keyVerse.quote: For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
keyVerse.note: This sentence explains everything else in the chapter: why Paul can be glad in chains, generous towards rivals, calm before a verdict that could mean death, and willing to postpone heaven for the church’s sake. If life means Christ, nothing can take it away, and death only brings more of him. It also searches every reader, because whatever else we put in the blank is lost at the grave.

1.reflection:
Paul is “sure” that God will complete the good work he began (v. 6). How does that confidence, resting on God’s faithfulness rather than our grip, change the way you face your own failures and the struggles of other believers?

Paul’s imprisonment advanced the gospel among the guards chained to him (vv. 12–14). What circumstance would you most like to change, and who is watching how you bear it?

Some preached Christ to hurt Paul, and he still rejoiced that Christ was proclaimed (vv. 15–18). When others succeed or get the credit, what does your reaction show about where your joy lies?

Complete the sentence honestly: “For to me to live is …” (v. 21). What would it look like this week for Christ, and not another good thing, to fill that blank, and for our church to stand side by side as citizens worthy of the gospel (v. 27)?

2.title: The Mind of Christ: Humility, the Incarnation, and the Cross
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 ended with a church under pressure from outside, called to stand firm together as citizens worthy of the gospel (1:27–30). Chapter 2 turns to the pressure inside: rivalry, conceit and grumbling, the kind of thing that later surfaces in two named women who cannot agree (4:2).

The message. Have the mind of Christ. The Son of God, who had every right, did not hold on to his rights but went down, all the way to a slave’s death on a cross, and God has lifted him to the name above every name. That mind is already theirs in him, and God is at work in them to make it show: in a church where each looks to the others’ interests, where no one mutters, and where ordinary people spend themselves for one another.

Why it was said. The Philippians were a generous, faithful church, but rivalry and grumbling were wearing at its unity, while its founder sat in chains (see the introduction). Paul’s answer is not a technique but a person.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–4 appeal for unity and humility on the ground of all they have received in Christ. Verses 5–11, one of the Bible’s great passages on the incarnation, set before them the mind of Christ, who emptied himself to the point of death on a cross and whom God has highly exalted. Verses 12–18 draw the consequences: work out your salvation, because God is working in you; stop grumbling, and shine like stars; Paul himself is glad to be poured out as an offering on their faith. Verses 19–30 show the same mind in two ordinary men: Timothy, who seeks their interests and not his own, and Epaphroditus, who nearly died in their service.

Where it leads. The chapter moves from the throne of God to a sickbed in Rome, and insists that they belong together. At its centre is the Lord who went lower than anyone and is now higher than all, given the name that Isaiah reserved for the LORD alone (Isaiah 45:23). He did not grasp; he gave; and the God who exalted him is the God now at work in his people.

For us. Ask where you are grasping at your rights, your standing or your opinion, and where you mutter instead of trusting. Then look at the Son who went down for you, and bow to him now, freely and gladly, as every knee one day will.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The mind that heals a divided church is the mind of Christ, and it is already theirs in him. Paul appeals to all they have received in Christ and asks for one mind and one love (vv. 1–2), and for a humility that counts others more significant and looks to their interests (vv. 3–4). That mind is theirs in Christ Jesus (v. 5), and Paul shows it in the Son, who, though truly God, did not use his rights for himself but emptied himself and obeyed to the point of death on a cross (vv. 6–8). Therefore God has exalted him as Lord, before whom every knee will bow, to the Father’s glory (vv. 9–11).
verseByVerse.theology:
What the Son Laid Aside, and What He Did Not

In verse 7 the emptying is explained by the taking of a servant’s form, so it is not subtraction but addition (see the note on v. 7, and the box “Where Christians differ: what did Christ empty himself of?” at the end of that note).

Verses 10–11 raise a second question: every knee bowing does not mean everyone is saved (see the box “Where Christians differ: will everyone be saved?” at the end of the note on vv. 9–11).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Philippi had a status problem. Paul’s vocabulary, eritheia, selfish ambition, suggests the quarrel of 4:2 was about position more than doctrine. Into that he drops the deepest thing he knows (see the note on v. 6).

Now: In most church conflicts the useful question is what you intend to do with the rights you have (see v. 6).

verseByVerse.quote: So if there is any encouragement in Christ, any comfort from love, any participation in the Spirit, any affection and sympathy, complete my joy by being of the same mind, having the same love, being in full accord and of one mind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since Christ has given them so much, they are to spend it on one another, one in mind and love, and so make Paul’s joy complete.

So if there is any encouragement in Christ. Four “if” clauses, and not one of them is in doubt: closer to “since there is” than to “if there happens to be”. Paul names what they already possess and then tells them what to do with it. “Encouragement” (paraklēsis), from calling someone alongside, is the strengthening that comes from union with Christ.

Comfort, participation, affection. “Comfort” (paramythion) is what you say quietly to someone who is grieving. “Participation” is koinōnia again (1:5), now in the Holy Spirit himself: shared life in the one Spirit. “Affection” is splanchna, the gut word of 1:8, and “sympathy” (oiktirmoi) is mercy that feels. These are not abstractions but the actual furniture of an ordinary Christian’s life.

No excuse for division. A church that had none of these might be forgiven for fragmenting. A church that has all four and still cannot get along has not run out of resources; it has declined to spend them.

Complete my joy. Paul, who rejoices in prison, over rivals, whatever the verdict, says his joy is not yet full, and the missing piece is not his release but their unity: he would rather have a united church in Macedonia than an open cell door in Rome. “Same mind” is to auto phronēte, think the same thing, and phroneō comes about ten times in Philippians. This is a letter about how Christians think, because how they think decides how they treat one another.

In full accord and of one mind. Four ways of saying it, a man leaning on a point, because there were tensions in the church (4:2). “Full accord” is sympsychoi, soul-joined. You can disagree with someone about a good deal and still be soul-joined to them, or agree about everything and be nothing of the kind.

Drawn into the oneness of God. The Father, the Son and the Spirit have lived for ever in perfect oneness, without rivalry or envy, and they have drawn sinners into that fellowship. The oneness God asks of us is the overflow of the oneness he has in himself, and the oneness Christ died to create.

In everyday life. If a relationship in your church has cooled, begin not with what the other person did but with what you have received in Christ. You are not asked to produce love from an empty account, but to spend from a full one: a word of encouragement, a kindness, a small act of mercy.

What if the other person will not be reconciled? You are responsible for your part, not theirs: “If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all” (Romans 12:18). Confess your own share of the fault without adding “but”, ask forgiveness, offer it freely, and speak to them rather than about them. If they refuse, keep your heart free from bitterness, keep praying, stay courteous, and leave the door open; sometimes a wise third person can help (Matthew 18:16). Unity is a gift of the Spirit to keep, not a result you can force, but you can make sure the wall is not being built from your side.

verseByVerse.quote: Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves. Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rivalry and the hunger to be admired divide a church; humility heals it by counting others more significant and caring for their interests as well as your own.

Selfish ambition or conceit. The two roots of division. “Selfish ambition” is eritheia, used of the rival preachers in 1:17: the self-seeking politician working a crowd. “Conceit” is kenodoxia, empty glory: wanting to be thought something more than wanting to be something. Neither announces itself. Nobody in Philippi was saying, “I am pursuing empty glory”. They were saying they had concerns about the direction of things, that certain people were not being listened to, that a principle was at stake. That is how eritheia always talks. It never uses its own name.

But in humility. Lowly-mindedness (tapeinophrosynē). In classical Greek the root was mostly an insult, a slave’s trait. The Old Testament had praised the lowly before God, and the church made Greece’s defect a virtue, because it had seen what Greece had not: God on a cross. Humility was a slave’s word until the Lord of glory wore it; now it is the family likeness of God’s children, because it is the likeness of their elder Brother.

Count others more significant than yourselves. To reckon, to judge a thing to be so (hēgeomai): the verb used of Christ in verse 6, who “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped”. Paul asks them to do the sum the way Christ did. It is an act of judgment, not a feeling, and you can do it on a Tuesday morning whatever you happen to feel.

But also to the interests of others. “Look” (skopeō) is to keep your eye on. The little word “also” keeps this healthy: your interests are real and you may attend to them; they are simply not the only ones in the room. A great deal of unhealthy Christian self-denial has been built by reading the verse as though that “also” were not there.

In everyday life. Think of the person in your church you find most difficult. Humility is not pretending you find them easy, nor concluding they are a better Christian than you. It is deciding, before the next conversation, that what they need from it matters more than what you want from it.

Does this mean I must let people walk all over me? No. Counting others more significant is a choice to serve, freely made, not a duty to be exploited. Jesus washed his disciples’ feet, and he also rebuked them, refused the crowd that wanted to make him king, and walked away from those who tried to throw him off a cliff. Looking to another’s interests sometimes means saying no, because indulging someone’s sin is not seeking their good. And this verse never requires anyone to remain under abuse. An abuser’s real interest is repentance, not continued power over you; the vulnerable must be protected, and wrongdoing brought into the light and, where it is a crime, reported. Humility serves; it does not enable evil.

Is this not a recipe for low self-esteem? No. Paul is not asking you to hold a low opinion of yourself but to stop needing an opinion of yourself at all. Low self-esteem and pride are both preoccupied with self: one says I am nothing, the other I am something, and both keep checking the score. The gospel settles the score from outside: if God has accepted you in Christ, his verdict is in, and you are free from the work of proving yourself. The humble person is not the one who thinks least of himself, but the one who no longer needs to think about himself in every room he enters.

verseByVerse.quote: Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mind Paul asks of the church is the mind of Christ, and it already belongs to them because they are in him. The letter turns on this short verse.

Have this mind among yourselves. “Mind” is phroneō again, and it is plural, addressed to the whole church: think this way, together. Paul is describing the culture of a congregation: what it feels like to be in that room, whose interests get raised in that meeting.

Which is yours in Christ Jesus. The mind of Christ is both our model and our possession (on the wording, see below), and the order matters. Take the verse as pure example and the hymn becomes a mountain to climb: be as humble as God was, a command that would crush anyone who took it seriously. Take it as union with Christ and his mind is already given to you, the air you now breathe, so live like it. That is Paul’s pattern everywhere: the command rests on the gift. Reverse them, so that the gift depends on keeping the command, and the gospel has become mere religion.

The Christ hymn. Verses 6–11, Christ’s descent (vv. 6–8) and exaltation (vv. 9–11), may be an early Christian hymn or Paul’s own composition. It is among the earliest and highest statements of Christ’s deity, written within about thirty years of the crucifixion. And Paul reaches for the incarnation to settle a squabble, which shows both how seriously he took the squabble and how practical he expected his highest doctrine to be.

What it does not mean. We cannot copy Christ’s atoning work. Nobody else empties himself from the form of God, and nobody else’s death redeems the world. We copy his attitude, and even that only because his atoning work has joined us to him.

Can I really have the mind of Christ? Yes, if you are in Christ, for the Spirit who lived in him lives in you, and “we have the mind of Christ” (1 Corinthians 2:16). It grows in three ways: by looking at him, in the Gospels, in this hymn, at the Lord’s Supper, for we are changed into the likeness of what we behold (2 Corinthians 3:18); by asking for it, since this is a work God delights to do (2:13); and by practising it in small decisions: the lower seat, the hidden service, the other person’s good. You will fail often. But it is already yours to grow into, not a foreign mind to be manufactured.

Uncertain wording. In Greek the second half of the verse has no verb, so translators must supply one. Older versions read: let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus; that is, imitate him. The ESV reads: which is yours in Christ Jesus; that is, this mind belongs to you because you are joined to him. The Greek allows either, and both are true: the ESV’s reading fits Paul’s habit of grounding commands in union with Christ, and the hymn plainly sets Christ before us as the pattern too.
verseByVerse.note: Verses 6–11 may be an early Christian hymn.

verseByVerse.quote: who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ was truly God, and he did not treat his equality with God as something to use for his own advantage. The hymn begins before Bethlehem, with the Son who shared the Father’s glory.

Though he was in the form of God. “Was” (hyparchōn) means existing: his continual state before the incarnation. Paul is describing not a man who was promoted but someone who was there first. Form (morphē) is not shape or appearance; it most likely means the outward expression of what something truly is. To be in the form of God is to be truly God, with his glory showing. All that makes God God belonged to the Son before he came; he speaks of the glory he had with the Father before the world existed (John 17:5). And “form” returns in verse 7: he who really was God really became a slave.

Did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped. The hinge of the hymn (on the wording, see below). The temptation he refused was not to become something he was not, but to use what he truly was for his own advantage. It was the temptation of the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–11): you are the Son of God, so use it, feed yourself, prove it, take the kingdoms now without the cross.

The second Adam. Adam, who was not God, grasped at being like God (Genesis 3:5). Christ, who was God, did not grasp. The Son shared the Father’s glory before there was a world; he did not need us, and he did not need to come. Where Adam grasped and fell, he opened his hands and stooped. The one who had a right to everything spent his rights on us, and is no less God for having done it.

Aimed at the quarrel. The question in a church fight is rarely whether I have a right here; usually you do. The question is what you do with the right you have. Christ, holding the highest rights in the universe, declined to press them for himself. Anyone who has been truly wronged in a congregation knows how much that costs, and how little like weakness it is.

If Jesus is God, how can he be distinct from the Father? This is the mystery of the Trinity. There is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4), and the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are each fully God, three persons sharing the one divine nature, distinct but never divided. The Son is not a part of God or a lesser god; he is equal with the Father in power and glory (the Westminster Confession 2.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 2.3). This hymn shows both truths: he was in the form of God, yet he obeyed the Father and was exalted by him. That obedience belongs to the work of salvation he freely took on as our Mediator; it does not make him eternally lower than the Father, whose glory he shares. We cannot fully understand how God is three and one, but we can worship, because this is how he has shown himself.

Uncertain wording. The noun behind “a thing to be grasped” is harpagmos, which occurs nowhere else in the New Testament; the root means to seize or snatch. The phrase can be read two ways: either he lacked equality with God and refused to snatch at it, or he possessed it and refused to exploit it for his own advantage. The line before has just said he was in the form of God, so most readers rightly take the second.

verseByVerse.quote: but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son emptied himself not by ceasing to be God but by becoming a servant: he took a full human nature and laid aside the glory that was his by right.

But emptied himself. To empty, pour out (ekenōsen); from it theology gets the word kenosis, which has been made to say things Paul did not say. Paul does not say what he emptied himself of. He says that he emptied himself, and then explains how: by taking the form of a servant. The emptying is not subtraction but addition. He did not become less God; he took to himself a human nature, a body, a mother, a birth, and with it laid aside not his deity but the free use of his divine rights for his own benefit. The glory was veiled, not surrendered; it broke out on a mountain (Matthew 17:2) to show it had been there all along. The Son who holds the universe together grew tired (John 4:6), needed sleep (Mark 4:38) and asked questions, because he had taken a real human life and would live it truly, depending on the Father and the Spirit.

By taking the form of a servant. The same word, form (morphē), as in verse 6: he became a servant as truly as he was God. Doulos, slave: Paul’s word for himself in 1:1, not modesty but imitation. Greek stories had gods appearing in human shape, but as disguises, and none told of a god choosing the slave’s place out of love. The Roman world had a ladder of status that every citizen spent his life climbing. Paul announces a God who came down the ladder, all the way, on purpose.

Being born in the likeness of men. “Likeness” (homoiōma) guards two truths. He was truly human, not God in a costume, made like us in every respect (Hebrews 2:17); yet not merely one more man, for he was without sin (Hebrews 4:15) and remained what he had always been. And “born” carries its own astonishment: the one who was in the form of God arrived as we all arrive, helpless, unable to lift his own head; the Creator was laid in a manger he had made. He did not lay aside his glory because he had too much of it, but because we had none: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

In everyday life. Look for one task this week that only a servant would do: the job nobody notices, the service nobody will thank you for, the person nobody else wants to help. Do it quietly, and remember who did it first, and for whom.

If Jesus was God, how could he not know the day of his return? Because he has two natures, divine and human, in one person. As God, the Son knows all things. As man, he had a true human mind that grew in wisdom (Luke 2:52) and knew what the Father gave him to know for his mission, so when he said he did not know the day (Mark 13:32), he spoke truly of his human knowledge. This is the wonder of the incarnation, not a contradiction: the eternal Son lived a human life from the inside, with its limits, and so he understands ours.

Where Christians differ: what did Christ empty himself of? Kenotic theories, held by some modern theologians, teach that the Son gave up divine attributes such as omniscience or omnipotence when he became man. This commentary’s view: the Son did not cease to be God or lose any divine attribute; God cannot stop being God. He emptied himself by taking human nature and the role of a servant, veiling his glory and not using his divine rights for his own benefit. He remained fully God while becoming fully man, two natures in one person, without confusion or change (the Chalcedonian Definition of AD 451; the Westminster Confession 8.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 8.2). He was not less than God in the manger, and not less than man on the cross.

parallels.desc: he poured out his soul to death

verseByVerse.quote: And being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having become man, Christ kept going down, by his own choice and in obedience to his Father, to the most shameful death the world knew. Verse 7 brought him from God to man; verse 8 takes him from man to a criminal’s execution.

Being found in human form. “Form” here is schēma, outward appearance. He looked like any other man. There was no halo in Nazareth.

He humbled himself. “Humbled” (tapeinoō) shares its root with the humility of verse 3. And he humbled himself: nothing was done to him that he did not accept. At his arrest and trial he looks passive, but he is descending on purpose: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18).

By becoming obedient to the point of death. Obedient to the Father, all the way (Hebrews 5:8): the eternal Son, in the work he had freely undertaken, submitting his human will to his Father’s in a garden at night, “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). And his obedience is counted as our righteousness: every day of that obedient life was lived on behalf of people who had not obeyed.

Even death on a cross. We have made the cross jewellery. Crucifixion was designed not merely to kill but to degrade: public, naked, slow. It was kept for slaves, rebels and the worst criminals, and Roman citizens, like many in Philippi, could not normally be crucified. Cicero said the very word cross should be kept far from the eyes, ears and thoughts of a Roman citizen.

The floor of the universe. Follow the line down: from the form of God, to the form of a slave, to death, to the death the empire kept for slaves and rebels, from the highest point there is to the lowest in the world he had made. And there is a depth the Romans could not see: to hang on a tree was to die under the curse of God’s own law (Deuteronomy 21:23), and he took that curse on himself to buy us out from under it (Galatians 3:13). That is the floor of the universe, and he touched it. He obeyed where we rebelled; he was cursed where we deserved to be; he was shamed so that we could be welcomed; he died the death of a slave so that slaves of sin could become sons of God.

What it does not mean. The cross was not only an example of humility; it was the atoning sacrifice for sin, once for all. But it is also the supreme example (see the note on v. 5). Set any grievance you are holding beside that descent and see whether it survives the comparison.

How can God die? God the Son did not stop existing, and the divine nature cannot die. But the Son had taken a true human nature, body and soul, and in that nature he truly died: his body was laid in the tomb and his spirit committed into his Father’s hands (Luke 23:46). Because the two natures belong to one person, Scripture can say that the Lord of glory was crucified (1 Corinthians 2:8) and that God obtained the church with his own blood (Acts 20:28): God the Son, in our flesh, dying our death.

Why did he have to die, and on a cross? Because our sin deserved the curse, and he came to bear it in our place. God is holy and just, and sin cannot simply be overlooked. At the cross the Father laid on his Son the penalty we owed: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). The cursed death of the tree showed what he carried, and the death of a slave how low love would go. This is called penal substitution (he bore our penalty as our substitute), and it is the heart of the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Crucifixion was the most shameful form of Roman execution.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the Son went down, God has lifted him to the highest place and given him the name of the LORD himself, so that all creation will confess him Lord, to the Father’s glory. The hymn turns on “therefore”: everything from verse 6 has been descent; from here it is all ascent.

Therefore God has highly exalted him. Jesus stated it as a law: “he who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11). “Highly exalted” (hyperypsoō) is super-exalted: resurrection, ascension, enthronement at God’s right hand (Acts 2:33; Ephesians 1:20–21). And notice who acts. On the way down, Christ did everything himself: he did not count, he emptied, he humbled. Now it is done to him. The Son did not lift himself; he went as far down as there is to go and left the raising to his Father, which is exactly what the quarrelling Philippians were failing to do. If you are busy exalting yourself, you have taken over the Father’s job.

The name that is above every name. Not “Jesus” in itself: that was a common name, and he had borne it from birth. Verse 11 tells us which: the coming confession is “Jesus Christ is Lord”. Kyrios, Lord, is the word the Greek Old Testament uses to render the divine name, Yahweh, the name devout Jews would not even pronounce. What is given to the risen Christ is God’s own name.

At the name of Jesus every knee should bow. The boldest thing in the letter. The words echo Isaiah 45:23: “To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear allegiance”, in a chapter that insists there is only one God: “I am the LORD, and there is no other” (Isaiah 45:5). Paul takes the homage God there reserves to himself alone, and says it is given to Jesus. It is hard to imagine a higher statement about Christ.

In heaven and on earth and under the earth. The whole of created reality: angels in heaven, humans on earth, and under the earth the dead, and perhaps demons. Every rational creature will bow.

Every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. One of the earliest Christian creeds (Romans 10:9; 1 Corinthians 12:3). In Philippi, a Roman colony, loyal subjects could call Caesar lord; to say Jesus is Lord was to say who really holds the throne. The hands that were nailed now hold the sceptre of the universe, and the name that was mocked over the cross is the name before which angels fall.

To the glory of God the Father. The Son’s exaltation is not a rival to the Father’s honour but the means of it (John 5:23). There is no competition inside the Trinity, no jockeying for position, which is precisely the disease Paul is treating in Philippi. He has shown them a God in whom there is no eritheia, no selfish ambition, at all, and asked them to live inside that.

What it does not mean. Jesus did not become God at his exaltation; he was always in the form of God (v. 6).

In everyday life. One day every knee will bow; a Christian is simply someone who has begun early. That turns the places where Jesus is not yet obeyed, your money, your tongue, your screen, your plans, into the next territory of his kingdom, and bowing there is not humiliation but homecoming.

Did Jesus earn his exaltation? In a sense, yes, as the Mediator, and that is good news for us. The Son did not need to earn his divine glory; he always had it (John 17:5). But as the God-man who finished the work the Father gave him, he received, in his human nature too, the honour due to that work, and not for himself alone but as the head of his people. Where he has gone, we will follow: “Because I live, you also will live” (John 14:19).

What does it mean to confess Jesus as Lord now? Saying freely now what everyone will say one day: “if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved” (Romans 10:9). It is more than words. It means owning him as your rightful King: trusting him to save you, obeying him when it costs, and naming him openly before others. To bow now is joy and life; to bow then, without having bowed now, is shame. The knee that bends today will never be ashamed.

Is it presumptuous to say every knee must bow to Jesus? Only if Christians were claiming that their side had won. But the one before whom every knee bows knelt to wash feet and went to a cross for his enemies. His lordship is the rule of the only one who has never misused power. And no Christian can boast of it, for every believer was once among the knees that would not bend, and bent only because grace bent them (1:29). The claim is not that we are better, but that he is Lord, and that he is good.

Where Christians differ: will everyone be saved? Some Christians, moved by the breadth of this vision, read it as meaning every person will eventually confess Christ willingly and be saved (universalism). This commentary’s view: every knee will bow and every tongue confess, but not all willingly or savingly. Some will confess in joyful worship; others will be compelled to acknowledge his lordship at the judgment (Romans 14:10–11; Revelation 20:11–15). Isaiah 45:24 adds that all who were incensed against him shall come to him and be ashamed. The letter itself forbids the universalist reading, speaking of the opponents’ destruction (1:28) and of those whose end is destruction (3:19). This is universal acknowledgement of Christ’s lordship, not universal salvation. Hell is real and eternal (Matthew 25:46). The question it puts to a reader is not whether you will acknowledge him, but when, and in which posture.
verseByVerse.note: The words echo a passage where the LORD says every knee will bow to him alone; Paul applies them to Jesus.

parallels.desc: to me every knee shall bow

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–18 — Working Out What God Works In
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because God is at work in them, they are to live out their salvation and shine in a dark world. With Paul absent, they are to go on working out what God has worked in, with reverent awe (vv. 12–13). That means an end to grumbling and disputing (v. 14), so that as blameless children of God they shine like stars in a twisted generation, holding to the word of life, and prove that Paul’s labour was not in vain (vv. 15–16). Even if his life is poured out like a drink offering on their faith, he is glad, and they should share his gladness (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology:
God’s Work and Ours

The decisive word in verses 12–13 is the small word “for” that joins them: God’s working is the source of our effort, not its rival, and it reaches beneath our obedience to our desires (see the note on vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Philippians had a good record of obedience, but it had been built with an apostle available. Now that he is in chains, the first sin he names is Israel’s sin in the wilderness: grumbling.

Now: For the believer who feels the gap between who he is and who he longs to be, verse 13 says the longing itself is God’s doing.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my beloved, as you have always obeyed, so now, not only as in my presence but much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Live out the salvation God has given you, seriously and reverently, because God himself is at work in you, giving both the desire and the power to obey.

Therefore, my beloved. Because Christ obeyed all the way down, and God raised him, therefore work. And Paul calls them beloved before he asks anything of them.

Much more in my absence. They have always obeyed, but that record was built with an apostle in the room. The real test is now, with him in a cell. Obedience that happens only when someone is watching is not yet obedience from the heart.

Work out your own salvation. Few verses have been more misread. First, “work out” is not “work for”. The verb (katergazesthe) means to carry a thing through to its finish, as a miner works out a seam of ore already in the ground. Nobody works for a salvation Paul has said God began and will complete (1:6). They are working out what has been worked in: letting the new life show in actual choices, the apology you make, the lie you refuse, the temper you hold (Colossians 3:9–10).

Together. Second, “your” is plural. “Your own salvation” sounds like a private project, but Paul is addressing a congregation with a quarrel in it, and working out includes working out their life together: not an anxious solo performance but a body at work in one another’s company.

With fear and trembling. Third, this is not terror of hell. Paul uses the phrase of his own weakness in Corinth (1 Corinthians 2:3) and of a slave’s service (Ephesians 6:5): reverent awe and humble dependence. The trembling is not the fear that God might drop you, but the awe of discovering that the holy God is at work in you, and that you had better not be careless in his workshop.

For it is God who works in you. Verse 13 gives the reason, and not the one we expect. Paul does not say, work hard, but remember God is also working, as though the two were rivals. He says: work, because God is working. God’s activity is the source of ours. The verb is energeō, to be at work, from which we get energy.

Both to will and to work for his good pleasure. Not merely the power to obey once you have decided, but the wanting too. So the Christian who finds in himself a real desire to please God is looking at evidence of God at work, not at his own good character: the wanting was a gift before the doing was. And he does it because it pleases him to. You are not a project he took on reluctantly.

The power that raised him. Christ became obedient to the point of death (2:8), and their obedience is his obedience being reproduced in them. The copy is never perfect, and need not be: his obedience, not theirs, is counted as their righteousness (Romans 5:19). And the God at work in them is the God who lifted the obedient Son from the cross to the throne; the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in every believer (Romans 8:11). So the desire to obey that you find in yourself this morning is God doing in you, in small, what he did at the empty tomb: making dead things live.

How do I know whether I am working out my salvation or just trying hard in my own strength? Look at what the effort leans on. Effort in your own strength is anxious, proud in success and despairing in failure, and it rarely prays. Working out what God has worked in begins in prayer, uses the means he gives (his word, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of the church), keeps going after failure because it rests on his promise, and thanks him for success. The test is not how hard you try but whom you are trusting while you try.

I feel the gap between who I am and who I long to be. Is God still working? Yes. The gap is not proof that God has left you to it; the longing itself is his. He is not waiting at the end of the road to see whether you make it; he is in you, producing both the appetite and the ability. Take the next small step of obedience in front of you, and thank him for the desire to take it.

Where Christians differ: God’s work and ours. Sanctification is the lifelong process by which God makes a forgiven person more and more like Christ (1 Thessalonians 4:3; 2 Corinthians 3:18). Some say it is all God’s work and we are passive; others that it is all our effort. This commentary’s view: God’s work and ours are both fully real. God works in us; therefore we work out. Our working is the result of his: not cooperation between equal partners, but our real activity flowing from his prior and deeper work (the Westminster Confession 16.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 16.3). We pray as if everything depends on God, because it does, and work because God is working.

verseByVerse.quote: Do all things without grumbling or disputing,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do everything without muttering against God or quarrelling with one another, because the God at work in you can be trusted with what you did not choose. After the throne, the cross and the name above every name, the first thing Paul applies the hymn to is grumbling.

Do all things without grumbling. “All things”: no exception, not the truly annoying, not the decision that really was wrong. “Grumbling” (gongysmos) is a low muttering, the word the Greek Old Testament uses again and again for Israel in the wilderness, murmuring about the water, the food, the leadership (Exodus 16:7–8; Numbers 14:27; 1 Corinthians 10:10). It turned a journey of weeks into forty years of funerals. God took it as an insult aimed past Moses at himself, because that is what it was.

Or disputing. “Disputing” (dialogismos) is the other half: the arguing, the endless reopening of decisions already made. Grumbling is what happens in the car on the way home; disputing is what happens in the meeting.

The respectable sin. A sin almost nobody repents of. It never gets anyone disciplined, it feels like honesty, it can even pass as discernment. But at root it is a complaint about how God is running things, delivered to a third party because it cannot be said aloud to him. The command comes straight after “it is God who works in you” because grumbling is the natural response of someone who believes he is on his own with circumstances he did not choose. Paul does not tell them to cheer up; he tells them God is with them and at work in them.

The Son who did not murmur. Israel grumbled about bread in the wilderness for forty years. Jesus went into the wilderness for forty days, and when the tempter offered bread, he answered with the lesson Israel had failed to learn: “Man shall not live by bread alone” (Matthew 4:4; Deuteronomy 8:3). Where they muttered, he trusted his Father. The Lord bore with a murmuring people for forty years and never stopped feeding them. His Son was silent before his accusers (Isaiah 53:7) and opened his mouth only to pray, to promise and to forgive. He bore the punishment for every complaint his people ever muttered against God, and from his silence came their peace.

In everyday life. This week, each time you catch yourself muttering, stop and turn it into a prayer, and then into thanks for one thing God has given in the same situation.

Is all complaining sin? No. Lament takes the pain to God, honestly, even angrily, and ends in trust: “How long, O LORD?” (Psalm 13:1), and then, “But I have trusted in your steadfast love” (Psalm 13:5). Grumbling takes the pain to everyone except God and ends in bitterness. Lament is faith in distress; grumbling is unbelief in conversation. So weep, ask, and pour out your heart to him. What you must refuse is the muttering that hardens into a settled grievance against God or his people.

How do I raise a real concern without grumbling? Take it to God first, and pray until your heart is no longer hot. Then take it to the person who can do something about it, not to everyone else (Matthew 18:15). Speak plainly and kindly, assume good motives where you honestly can, and offer to help. Then accept the outcome graciously, even if you still disagree, unless conscience or sin is at stake. A concern raised this way builds a church; the same concern muttered in the car park tears it down.

verseByVerse.quote: that you may be blameless and innocent, children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and twisted generation, among whom you shine as lights in the world, holding fast to the word of life, so that in the day of Christ I may be proud that I did not run in vain or labor in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A church that stops grumbling and holds to the gospel shines like stars in a dark world, and proves that Paul’s labour was not wasted. The purpose of the command is far larger than a quieter church.

Blameless and innocent. “Blameless” (amemptos): no just cause for blame. “Innocent” (akeraios): unmixed, pure, like wine not watered down or metal without alloy.

Children of God without blemish. “Without blemish” (amōmos) is what a sacrificial animal had to be to be offered at all. And Paul gives them the name before the description: children of God. It is not a title earned by being blameless; it is who they are, and blamelessness is the family likeness (1 Peter 1:15).

In the midst of a crooked and twisted generation. A quotation from the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:5), where the crooked generation is Israel, God’s own people in the wilderness, murmuring. Paul applies it to the unbelieving world, just after warning the church against the sin that earned Israel the label. And “in the midst”: believers live in the middle of it, not withdrawn from it.

Among whom you shine as lights in the world. “Lights” (phōstēres) is not the word for a lamp but the word Genesis 1:14–16 uses for the sun, moon and stars (compare Daniel 12:3). A small church in a Roman colony is set into the dark like a star, visible for the same reason stars are: because it is dark. The darkness does not defeat the light; it makes it plain to see (Matthew 5:14–16). And a star does not lecture: it simply is what it is, and anyone who looks up can see it. Paul’s picture of witness here is first of all not a message spoken but a community people can see, which is why the command that produces it was about grumbling. A church that does not mutter is already preaching something to a city that does.

Holding fast to the word of life. The church clings to the gospel for its own life and holds it out to a world that has none (on the wording, see below), and it cannot do the second for long without the first.

That I did not run in vain or labor in vain. The runner and the labourer. Paul admits that on the last day he wants something to show for his life, not to be admired, but so that his running was not for nothing. This is a pastor’s ambition converted: the people are the prize.

Without blemish because he was. The New Testament uses the phrase above all of Christ, who “offered himself without blemish to God” (Hebrews 9:14). Only his life was ever fit for the altar on its own merits, and he has reconciled his people by his death, “in order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him” (Colossians 1:22). So the call is not to supply what only the Lamb could supply, but to become in daily life what his sacrifice has made them before God.

Not an orphan. We are all God’s creatures, but sonship is a gift: “to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12). Notice why Paul says it right after grumbling. A grumbler lives like an orphan: nobody is looking after him, so he must look after himself and complain when it goes wrong. Timothy Keller pointed out in The Prodigal God that the elder brother in Jesus’ parable lived like that inside his father’s house: he obeyed to get the father’s goods rather than to enjoy the father, and when short-changed he stood outside and sulked. The answer is the Son. God sent him “so that we might receive adoption as sons” (Galatians 4:5), treated as an outcast on the cross so that outcasts could be brought into the family. To each of them the Father says, “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (Luke 15:31). So when the muttering starts this week over the rota or the bill, say it plainly: I am not an orphan; my Father knows. See Adoption in the Theological Dictionary.

In everyday life. Think of the darkest place you will be this week: the office culture, the group chat, the family gathering. Decide one thing you will refuse to do there (join the grumbling, the gossip, the cynicism) and one thing you will do (an honest word, a kindness, a word about Christ if the door opens).

Should Christians withdraw from a corrupt world? No. Stars shine in the night sky, not in a bunker, and Jesus prayed not that his people would be taken out of the world, but kept from the evil one (John 17:15). Guard your heart and choose your closest influences wisely, but do not mistake isolation for holiness. A light hidden under a basket has not been kept pure; it has simply stopped being a light.

How do I shine without being self-righteous? Remember that the light is borrowed: Christ is the light of the world, you shine as the moon does, by reflecting him, and you were part of the crooked generation yourself until he called you. So be honest about your own failures; humility is part of the shine. Be kind, generous, truthful and cheerful, and do not grumble about the culture as though you were better than it. And when people ask, point them to the source of the light rather than to yourself.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “holding fast” (epechontes) can mean either to hold on firmly or to hold out, to offer. The ESV takes the first; the King James Version’s “holding forth” takes the second, which suits the picture of lights shining on the world. Both are possible, and Paul may mean both.

parallels.desc: those who are wise shall shine

verseByVerse.quote: Even if I am to be poured out as a drink offering upon the sacrificial offering of your faith, I am glad and rejoice with you all. Likewise you also should be glad and rejoice with me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even if Paul’s life ends in execution, he counts it a glad offering poured out on their faith, and he asks them to rejoice with him.

Poured out as a drink offering. Wine poured out with a sacrifice (Numbers 28:7), the last small act completing an offering someone else had brought. Paul uses the image again when his death has become a certainty: “For I am already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure has come” (2 Timothy 4:6). The Gentiles in Philippi knew the picture anyway: a little wine poured out to the gods was part of nearly every Greek and Roman sacrifice and formal meal. Paul’s offering is his own life, poured out to the one true God.

Upon the sacrificial offering of your faith. Paul is not the sacrifice. Their faith and service are the sacrifice (Romans 12:1), the main event on the altar; his own violent death, if it comes, is only the cup of wine poured over the top. And the picture makes his execution an act of worship, not a political accident. Rome thinks it is disposing of a troublemaker; Paul sees a priest at an altar.

I am glad and rejoice with you all. Four verbs of joy in two verses, on the subject of his own execution. This is not stoicism, which grits its teeth and feels nothing, and it is not denial. It is the settled gladness of a man who worked the question out in chapter 1, “to die is gain”, and has nothing left to fear.

You also should be glad and rejoice with me. The harder half, as anyone knows who has sat with a dying Christian more at peace than the family around the bed. Grief is not forbidden (v. 27), but he refuses to let the church treat his death as a defeat, because it is not one.

Poured out after him. Paul can speak calmly of being poured out because someone was poured out first. The Servant in Isaiah “poured out his soul to death” (Isaiah 53:12), and at the Last Supper Jesus took the cup and said, “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many” (Mark 14:24). That pouring was the sacrifice itself, the one offering that takes away sin; Paul’s would be only a cup of thanks spilled beside it. A man who has drunk from the cup of the new covenant in Christ’s blood is willing, if God wills, to see his own life poured out on the same altar, and to call it joy.

What it does not mean. Paul’s death would atone for nothing. Christ’s sacrifice is the only atoning sacrifice, offered once for all (Hebrews 10:10–14). What believers offer is thanks, not atonement: their faith, their service, their bodies, and if God wills, their lives.

In everyday life. Ask what in your ordinary life could be an offering to God: today’s work, the care you give a child or a parent, the money in your account, the hours of a hard week. Offer it to him in so many words this morning.

Was Paul in fact martyred? Not at this point, it seems. He expected release (1:25; 2:24), and the letters to Timothy and Titus suggest he was freed and travelled again. Early Christian tradition says he was later imprisoned again and beheaded in Rome under Nero, in the mid-60s AD. 2 Timothy shows the drink offering finally being poured, and Paul still at peace.

How can I rejoice when a Christian I love is dying? You do not have to choose between grief and joy; in a believer they can run together. Weep, because death is an enemy and parting hurts. And rejoice, because for them it is gain, and their life has been an offering God accepted. Tell them what their faith has meant to you. Pray with them, read them the promises, sing if they want to sing. The joy comes not by forcing it but by looking at death from the dying believer’s side, as Paul asks, and seeing Christ waiting there.
verseByVerse.note: A drink offering was wine poured out with a sacrifice, completing it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–30 — Two Men Who Show You the Mind of Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The mind of Christ is not only a doctrine but a life, and Paul shows it in two men the Philippians know. Timothy, unlike those who seek their own interests, is genuinely concerned for them and has proved himself serving with Paul like a son with his father; Paul will send him soon, and hopes to come himself (vv. 19–24). Epaphroditus nearly died serving Paul on their behalf; Paul sends him home to be welcomed with joy, and asks them to honour such men (vv. 25–30).
verseByVerse.theology:
Virtue Has to Be Seen in a Face

After the doctrine, Paul gives a person. Timothy embodies 2:4, looking to the interests of others, and Epaphroditus embodies 2:7–8, pouring himself out to the point of nearly dying. Neither is presented as exceptional. They are what the gospel ordinarily produces in people it has got hold of.

Paul also admits to sorrow, and to sorrow that could have been piled upon sorrow (see the note on vv. 25–27).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Epaphroditus was returning early, ill and with the job unfinished, and Paul heads off wrong conclusions before the man reaches the gate (see the note on vv. 25–27).

verseByVerse.quote: I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, so that I too may be cheered by news of you. For I have no one like him, who will be genuinely concerned for your welfare.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul hopes to send Timothy soon, because no one else shares his genuine care for them as Timothy does. After the hymn come travel arrangements, and that is not an anticlimax but the point: the Philippians did not need another idea; they needed a face, a man in whom the mind of Christ could be seen.

I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy. Even the travel plan is submitted to Christ: Paul knows the Lord may decide otherwise (v. 23).

So that I too may be cheered by news of you. To be in good heart (eupsycheō), a verb found nowhere else in the New Testament. The man who rejoices in prison admits that he needs cheering up, and that news from this church would do it. Contentment in Paul is never self-sufficiency. He needed people.

I have no one like him. Of equal soul, like-minded (isopsychos): nobody else is of one soul with Paul. What makes Timothy unique is not his ability but his care.

Genuinely concerned for your welfare. “Genuinely” (gnēsiōs) comes from a root meaning true-born, legitimate: not the counterfeit. Plenty of people can produce concern when the situation calls for it; Timothy’s was the real thing. He embodies the humble mind Paul asked for, looking to the interests of others (2:4): the command walking about in a body, and a small copy of the Son who looked to our interests all the way to the cross (2:6–8).

The gift Paul could least spare. There is a quiet rebuke in the arrangement. Paul is sending his most valuable colleague, the one man of his own soul, at the moment he can least spare him. A church arguing about who ranks where is about to receive, as a gift, the person its founder could least afford to give away. And behind Paul stands the Shepherd who never seeks his own interests at our expense, and who gave us what he could least spare: his own life.

If Christ is enough, why did Paul need cheering up? Because Christ is enough in a way that includes his people, not excludes them. God made us to need one another, and he often sends his comfort through them: “God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus” (2 Corinthians 7:6). Needing friends is not a failure of faith; it is how the body of Christ is designed. If you are lonely and low, it is not unspiritual to say so, or to ask for company.

verseByVerse.quote: For they all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. But you know Timothy’s proven worth, how as a son with a father he has served with me in the gospel. I hope therefore to send him just as soon as I see how it will go with me, and I trust in the Lord that shortly I myself will come also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy stands out because those around Paul were busy with their own affairs, while he has proved himself in years of serving alongside Paul like a son with his father. Paul will send him once the verdict is known, and trusts the Lord to let him come himself.

For they all seek their own interests. A bleak sentence. Paul cannot mean every Christian in Rome (1:14), and Epaphroditus was faithful; he most likely means everyone available for this errand. Even so, we should let the sentence stay hard. The apostle to the Gentiles looked for someone who would put a distant congregation ahead of his own convenience, and found one man. And he does not say they sought sin, but their own interests, the phrase of verse 4. These were not scandalous people, only ordinary Christians with their own things to get on with, and that was enough to disqualify them. Self-interest does not need to be dramatic to be deadly.

Not those of Jesus Christ. The hymn has just shown what his interests are: he did not please himself (Romans 15:3), but gave himself for people who had no claim on him. Seeking them is not adding a religious hobby to a busy life but caring about what he cares about: a distant congregation’s welfare, the weak brother, the progress of the gospel. Timothy’s concern for the Philippians was the shape his devotion to Christ took.

Timothy’s proven worth. Tested character (dokimē), metal that has been through the assayer’s fire: not promise or potential, but what has been tested, and the Philippians had watched it happen (Acts 16:1–3).

As a son with a father he has served with me. Paul changes his sentence halfway through. “As a son with a father” would naturally end “he has served me”, but he will not say that. He writes instead, “he has served with me in the gospel”: not under Paul but alongside him, both of them slaves (douleuō) of the same Master. That change of course says more about how Paul regarded the younger man than a paragraph of praise would.

As soon as I see how it will go with me. The trial is still undecided, and Paul wants Timothy to carry definite news once the outcome is known. Yet he expects release, as he reasoned in 1:24–25, and the confidence is carefully hedged, “I trust in the Lord”, by a man who might be poured out as a drink offering (2:17). He holds both without strain, which is what hope looks like when it has stopped needing certainty.

In everyday life. A diary is an honest confession: it shows whose interests filled last week. Somewhere in your week is a task nobody wants, a visit, a gift, an hour of prayer for missions, that could be done purely for the interests of Jesus Christ. And think of a Christian carrying a heavy load, and send them good news this week; you may be the cheer they need.

Isn’t everyone really out for themselves? A good deal of modern thought says so. Economics often models people as rational self-interest on two legs; popular evolutionary accounts explain kindness as a strategy for passing on genes; and the novelist Ayn Rand called one of her books The Virtue of Selfishness (1964), arguing that self-sacrifice is a betrayal of yourself. Paul’s sentence agrees with such cynics more than the idealist does: left to ourselves, that is where we drift. But the cynic cannot explain Timothy, a young man “genuinely concerned” for people far away, with nothing to gain. Still less can he explain the Son of God, who had everything and emptied himself for people who had no claim on him (vv. 6–8). That is the surprise of the gospel: more pessimistic about the human heart than the optimist, and more hopeful than the cynic, because the self-giving of Christ, once it reaches a person, starts to reproduce itself.

How do I know if I am seeking my own interests rather than Christ’s? Look at the ordinary choices, because that is where these Christians failed. When a need arises that would cost you time or comfort, what is your first reaction? Do you serve only where you will be seen or thanked? Are your plans shaped by Christ’s kingdom, or by what suits you, with Christ fitted in around the edges? Seeking his interests does not mean neglecting your family or work; those are part of his interests. It means asking, before you decide, what would serve him and his people, and being willing for the answer to cost you.

How do I find a Timothy, or become one? Spiritual fathers and sons, mothers and daughters, are formed by shared life, not just shared classes. If you are older in the faith, invite a younger believer to pray and serve alongside you and see how you handle real situations; if you are younger, ask a mature Christian whether you can spend time with them. Paul took Timothy on his journeys (Acts 16:3). Proven worth is built over years of faithfulness in small things, watched by someone who loves you enough to tell you the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: I have thought it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus my brother and fellow worker and fellow soldier, and your messenger and minister to my need, for he has been longing for you all and has been distressed because you heard that he was ill. Indeed he was ill, near to death. But God had mercy on him, and not only on him but on me also, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul sends Epaphroditus home with high honour: a faithful brother who nearly died in their service, and whose recovery was God’s mercy to him and to Paul.

Epaphroditus. He had brought the Philippians’ gift to Paul (4:18), and had probably been sent to stay and serve. Now Paul sends him home, probably carrying this letter, early, ill and empty-handed, and everyone in Philippi will have a view about that. So Paul, before the man arrives, builds him a reputation. He is not returning a failure. He is returning a soldier.

My brother and fellow worker and fellow soldier. Five titles in one sentence, and they climb: brother, family; fellow worker, the same task; fellow soldier, the same danger, no mere figure of speech, since the man nearly died getting to Paul. Then two that belong to the Philippians. “Messenger” is apostolos, sent one: their envoy. “Minister” is leitourgos, priestly servant, from the same root as the offering of verse 17: their gift, carried by this man, was an act of worship.

Distressed because you heard that he was ill. Near death, he was troubled not by his own condition but by their worry. The word (adēmoneō) is strong: deeply troubled, the word used of Jesus in Gethsemane (Mark 14:33). Here is the mind of Christ at the level of a sickbed: a dangerously ill man whose distress was for the people distressed about him.

But God had mercy on him. No hint that the illness was a failure of somebody’s prayers; the recovery is credited entirely to mercy. And Paul extends the mercy to himself, “lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow”: the man who wrote “to die is gain” admits that he was already carrying sorrow, and that losing this friend would have piled more on top. Grief is not unbelief. Paul’s joy was never the absence of grief; it ran underneath it. And the Lord who was distressed in Gethsemane bore the sorrow upon sorrow that our sin deserved, so that no grief of his people would be without hope.

What it does not mean. Healing is not automatic for those with faith, and when a believer is not healed, it does not mean God has been unmerciful or someone’s faith was weak. Sometimes God’s mercy is recovery; sometimes it is taking his child home, which is far better (1:23).

In everyday life. If someone in your church is ill, pray for them by name, and visit, call or write this week. And if you are the one who is ill, let people care for you; that, too, is part of the fellowship of the body.

Why did Paul not simply heal him? Even the apostles could not heal at will; the signs were God’s to give, not theirs to command. An apostle through whom God healed others (Acts 19:11–12) watched his friend nearly die, and he left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). The miraculous gifts were signs given through the apostles to confirm the gospel in its foundation (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4), and we hold that such sign gifts have ceased, while God still heals in answer to prayer as he wills. Many faithful Christians and whole churches that pray for healing and practise spiritual gifts read these passages differently, and they are our brothers and sisters in Christ. So Christians today should pray for the sick in faith, use the means God gives, including medicine, and leave the outcome to his mercy, as Paul did here.

Is it unspiritual to be deeply distressed, or even depressed? No. Epaphroditus was deeply troubled; Paul expected sorrow upon sorrow; Jesus himself was greatly distressed in Gethsemane and said, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death” (Mark 14:34). Overwhelming distress is not in itself sin or a lack of faith. Bring it to God honestly, as the psalmists did, and let other believers help you carry it. If low mood persists or deepens, talk to your pastor and seek out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up: body and mind are both God’s creation, and receiving the treatment a doctor recommends is no more unspiritual than Paul’s concern for Epaphroditus’s recovery. If you have thoughts of ending your life, do not wait: tell someone and get medical help the same day.
verseByVerse.note: Epaphroditus had brought the Philippians’ gift to Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: I am the more eager to send him, therefore, that you may rejoice at seeing him again, and that I may be less anxious.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul hurries Epaphroditus home so that the church can rejoice to see him, and Paul himself will carry one sorrow fewer.

I am the more eager to send him. The word carries urgency: Paul is not waiting for his own affairs to settle, which is very likely why this letter was written when it was. And he explains the return twice, in verse 26 and here, so that nobody in Philippi can assemble a story about a man who gave up and came home. Protecting a servant’s reputation before he arrives is an unglamorous kind of love, and every church needs it.

That I may be less anxious. Literally, less sorrowful. The man who will write “do not be anxious about anything” (4:6) has real cares, a friend’s health, a frightened congregation, a capital trial with no date set, and does what he can to reduce them. Freedom from anxiety in Paul is never the absence of things worth worrying about, but what a man does with them.

The mind of Christ in a travel plan. He needs Epaphroditus; they need to see him alive; so he sends him (2:4). Christ’s mind is seen when a prisoner gives away the friend sent to care for him so that a church can stop grieving.

How can Paul be anxious and yet tell me not to be? Two different things go under the same English word. Concern is the right weight of love for people and situations God has given you: Paul speaks of “the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches” (2 Corinthians 11:28). Sinful anxiety is fretting that takes the burden away from God and carries it alone, imagining the worst and trusting nothing. Paul’s way was to feel the concern fully, pray about it, do the practical thing within his power, and leave the rest with God, exactly what 4:6–7 commands. You will still feel concern; the question is where you take it.

verseByVerse.quote: So receive him in the Lord with all joy, and honor such men, for he nearly died for the work of Christ, risking his life to complete what was lacking in your service to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Welcome Epaphroditus with joy and honour people like him, for he risked his life for Christ’s work to give Paul the help the church could not give in person.

So receive him in the Lord with all joy. Paul is still managing the homecoming: no cool reception at the gate, no disappointment that he came home early, no unspoken question about why. Welcome him in the Lord, as a brother in Christ, not as an employee who failed to complete his contract.

Honour such men. Make it your policy to hold people like this in honour, Paul tells a church with a status problem. Paul has spent the chapter dismantling the pursuit of empty glory, and he does not finish by abolishing honour. He redirects it: not to the impressive, the gifted or the visibly successful, but to the man who nearly died on an errand and has nothing to show for it.

Risking his life. Staking, throwing your money onto the table (paraboleuomai, a gambler’s term): he staked his life. Centuries later in Alexandria a brotherhood of Christians who nursed the sick, plague victims among them, was called the parabolani, a name usually traced to the same root: not recklessness, but a deliberate bet that a life is worth staking on Christ’s work.

To complete what was lacking in your service to me. Not a rebuke. The Philippians had given generously; what was lacking was the one thing they could not send: themselves. Epaphroditus went in their place, filling the gap with his own body, their hands arriving where they could not.

The chapter ends on the ground. It opened with the Son of God taking the form of a slave; it closes with an unremarkable Christian from a provincial church gambling his life to carry a gift to a prisoner, and Paul means the comparison. The mind of Christ is mostly worked out by people whose names would otherwise never have been recorded.

He supplied what was lacking. Christ staked everything, knowing exactly what it would cost, and paid it in full. He went in our place where we could not go, and supplied with his own body all that was lacking in our service to God. And now he honours his servants, welcomes them home with joy, and remembers every risk taken in his name. One day he will say “well done” to people nobody else ever thought to praise.

How should we honour people like this without creating celebrities? As Paul does here: welcome them warmly, speak well of them, tell their story truthfully so that people praise God for them, care for their needs, and listen to them. Honour the quiet servants especially: the carer, the volunteer, the missionary back from a hard place, the believer who lost a job for the faith. Honour should point beyond them to Christ, whose work they did; the danger is honouring the wrong things in them: gifts and visibility instead of faithfulness and sacrifice.

What does risking for Christ look like for an ordinary Christian? For some it is literal: believers in hostile countries, missionaries in dangerous places, doctors and nurses who serve where disease is rife. For most of us it is smaller but real: a friendship risked by speaking of Christ, a career by refusing to lie, comfort by caring for someone difficult or ill. Epaphroditus did not seek danger; he took on a task for Christ and did not let the danger stop him. Ask not how to be heroic, but what task Christ has given you that you have been avoiding because it might cost you.

Textual note. The King James Version’s “not regarding his life” follows later manuscripts, which have a similar-looking word.

keyVerse.quote: Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus
keyVerse.note: This verse joins the two halves of the chapter’s first section: the call to humble unity (vv. 1–4) and the portrait of Christ who emptied himself and was exalted (vv. 6–11). It tells us that the mind Paul asks for is not one we must manufacture but one we already have in Christ, and everything that follows, from working out our salvation to the lives of Timothy and Epaphroditus, shows that mind at work.

2.reflection:
Paul grounds his appeal for unity in what believers already have: encouragement in Christ, comfort from love, participation in the Spirit, affection and sympathy (v. 1). Which of these do you most need to remember when a relationship in church is strained, and what would it look like to “spend” it?

Christ did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself (vv. 6–7). Where are you most tempted to insist on your rights, your reputation or your way, and what would it mean to open your hands?

Verses 12–13 tell us to work out our salvation because God is at work in us. How does this change the way you think about effort, failure and growth in your Christian life?

Paul calls the church to do all things without grumbling (v. 14), and shows the mind of Christ in the ordinary service of Timothy and Epaphroditus (vv. 19–30). Where do you need to turn muttering into prayer, and whom could you serve or honour this week as they did?

3.title: Knowing Christ: The Surpassing Worth and the Pressing Forward
3.overview:
Where we are. After the mind of Christ seen in Paul’s co-workers (chapter 2), chapter 3 turns to a sharp warning and a personal testimony, from which the call to stand firm in chapter 4 grows.

The message. Christ is enough, and everything else is loss beside him. Nothing you are or achieve can make you right with God; to be found in Christ, with a righteousness God gives through faith, is all you need, and knowing him is worth more than anything you could lose. Yet having him is not arriving: those whom Christ has taken hold of run hard after him, until he comes from heaven to finish what he began, even in their bodies.

Why it was said. Travelling teachers were telling Gentile believers that faith in Christ was not enough: they must also be circumcised and keep the law of Moses (see the introduction). Others professed Christ while living for their appetites. One danger added to the cross; the other ignored it, and Paul answers both.

How the chapter makes its case. Paul calls the church to rejoice in the Lord and warns against those who add circumcision to Christ (vv. 1–3). Then his own story: if anyone could have earned God’s approval by pedigree and performance, it was Saul of Tarsus, and all of it he now counts as loss, even rubbish, beside knowing Christ and being found in him (vv. 4–11). Then he guards against the opposite error: he has not arrived, but presses on like a runner because Christ has made him his own (vv. 12–16). Finally he sets his example against the enemies of the cross, whose god is their belly, and reminds the citizens of a Roman colony that their real citizenship is in heaven (vv. 17–21).

Where it leads. The centre of the chapter is a person: “knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (v. 8). He is the believer’s righteousness (v. 9); his sufferings and resurrection shape the believer’s life (v. 10); he seized Paul on the Damascus road and waits at the end of the race (v. 12); and he will make our lowly bodies like his glorious body (v. 21). The Christ who was humbled and exalted in chapter 2 will lift his people by the same road.

For us. Finish the sentence “God accepts me because of Christ, and…”, and set down whatever comes after the “and”. Then ask where your mind settles when nothing is demanding its attention, and whether your life is running toward him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Everything I Had, and What It Was Worth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joy in Christ leaves no room for anything added to him, because he is worth more than everything else together. Paul calls the church to rejoice in the Lord and warns them against teachers who insist on circumcision, for the true people of God boast in Christ and trust nothing in themselves (vv. 1–3). His own record was better than theirs (vv. 4–6), yet he counts all of it loss, even rubbish, for the surpassing worth of knowing Christ (vv. 7–8), of being found in him with a righteousness from God through faith (v. 9), and of sharing his sufferings on the way to the resurrection (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification: A Righteousness From Outside

Against a righteousness of his own stands a righteousness that comes from God and is received through faith, Christ’s record credited to those who are in him (this is treated fully in the note on v. 9). Verse 11 is not doubt (see the note on v. 11).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Judaizers (teachers demanding circumcision) offered the Philippians an addition to Christ: faith plus circumcision, grace plus performance. Paul answers from his own life: he had every credential they prized, more than any of them, and beside Christ it all went out with the kitchen refuse.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. To write the same things to you is no trouble to me and is safe for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Make the Lord himself your joy, and welcome the repeated warning that keeps that joy safe.

Finally, my brothers. Paul is not winding up: two chapters remain, and the sharpest passage in the letter is about to begin. The phrase (to loipon) means “as for the rest”, turning to a new subject (1 Thessalonians 4:1). The change of tone is explained by the danger Paul is about to name, not by a second letter stitched in (see the introduction).

Rejoice in the Lord. A command, as again in 4:4. Can anyone be ordered to feel something? The command is not “be cheerful” but “rejoice in the Lord”: it names someone to rejoice in, not a mood. Paul is telling them to look at someone, on the reasonable assumption that joy will follow the looking.

The place you stand. Paul’s joy does not rest on his circumstances (a cell and a pending capital charge), the health of the church (which has a quarrel in it), or the absence of enemies. Christian joy is not the conclusion you reach after surveying your situation; it is the place you stand while you survey it, for the Lord we rejoice in does not change (Hebrews 13:8). And it is the first defence against what follows: those who rejoice in Christ do not need anything added to him, which is exactly what the teachers of verse 2 were offering.

The same things. Paul is not afraid of boring them. Repeating himself costs him nothing (“no trouble to me”) and keeps them safe (asphales, secure). Repetition is not a teacher’s failure of imagination. It is the handrail on the stair (compare 2 Peter 1:12–13).

A Lord who was bound. The Lord is Jesus, before whom every knee will bow, the one who emptied himself, went to a cross, and was raised and exalted (2:6–11). And he knows the place Paul writes from. He too was arrested and bound (John 18:12), brought before a Roman governor and condemned, and none of it unseated him as Lord. A prisoner can rejoice in such a Lord, because his chains are not the end of his story, any more than his Lord’s were.

How do I rejoice in the Lord when I feel nothing, or feel low? Begin with the object, not the feeling: turn your attention to him, read about him, remember what he has done, sing or say back to him what is true. Feelings often follow slowly, sometimes a long way behind. The psalmists talked to their own souls: why are you cast down, O my soul? Hope in God (Psalm 42:5). Joy in Scripture can sit alongside tears, illness and grief; it is a settled gladness in God rather than a constant mood.
