And if low mood is deep and lasting, talk to your pastor and seek out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up; if the doctor recommends treatment, receiving it is no failure of faith. God uses both.

Why do I need to hear the same truths over and over? Because we forget, and because the truths that matter most are deep enough never to be exhausted. The things a Christian most needs to hear are almost never new: the same handful of truths, driven in again, because we leak. Paul refuses to be too sophisticated to say a thing twice, and a sermon on a familiar text is no reason to feel cheated.

Uncertain wording. Paul does not say what “the same things” are: the call to rejoice, which he repeats in 4:4, or the warning that follows, which he says he has often given before (v. 18). The warning fits “safe for you” best, but either way, what protects believers is worth saying again.

verseByVerse.quote: Look out for the dogs, look out for the evildoers, look out for those who mutilate the flesh. For we are the circumcision, who worship by the Spirit of God and glory in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beware of anyone who adds circumcision to Christ, for the true people of God are those who worship by the Spirit, boast in Christ and trust nothing in themselves.

Look out for the dogs. The tone changes without warning: three times blepete, look out, and three stinging names for the same people. Dogs were half-wild scavengers on the rubbish heaps, and “dog” could be a Jewish insult for a Gentile: the outsider, unclean. Paul turns the word round. Those insisting that Gentiles must be circumcised to belong, the Judaizers, are themselves the dogs, scavenging at the edge of a covenant they have not understood. They may not yet have reached Philippi; Paul is probably warning in advance, because such teachers had already troubled Antioch and Galatia (Acts 15:1; Galatians 1:6–7; 5:2–12), and a young Gentile church was exactly where they would go next.

Look out for the evildoers. Literally the evil workers. They prided themselves on works of the law; Paul calls their works evil, because works offered to God as the reason he should accept us are not obedience. They compete with Christ.

Those who mutilate the flesh. A pun lost in English. Circumcision is peritomē, a cutting around; Paul calls their practice katatomē, a hacking, the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the pagan gashing the law forbade (Leviticus 21:5; 1 Kings 18:28). Circumcision was a sign pointing to a heart made new by God. Demanded as a condition of salvation, it points to nothing: it is only a cut in the body.

For we are the circumcision. Not something like it: it. A congregation of mostly uncircumcised Macedonian Gentiles is told they are the covenant people, and the men pressing the knife are not. Believers in Christ, Jew and Gentile, are circumcised in heart by the Spirit (Romans 2:28–29). God himself has cut away the hard heart and given a new one (Ezekiel 36:26), as Moses had promised: “the LORD your God will circumcise your heart” (Deuteronomy 30:6).

Worship by the Spirit. Three marks define the true circumcision, a fair test of any church or any soul. First, worship by the Spirit of God. “Worship” (latreuō) is the word for the temple service, and to worship by the Spirit is to depend on the one who opens our eyes to Christ and moves our hearts to love God, not on ritual or technique (John 4:23–24). So a plain prayer from a believing heart at a kitchen table is true worship, and a flawless ceremony from a heart that trusts itself is not.

Glory in Christ Jesus. Second, the boast (kauchaomai) has moved outside the self altogether, to the one person the sign pointed to (Galatians 6:14). Believers were circumcised by the circumcision of Christ (Colossians 2:11), which many take to mean his death, when he was cut off for his people. The Judaizers were demanding a cutting that only pointed to a death Christ had already died. To glory in Christ Jesus is to stop offering God anything done by you or to you, and to rest in what Christ did.

No confidence in the flesh. Third, and this one searches us, because flesh is broader than circumcision: status, achievement, religious performance, anything you could offer as a reason God should accept you, your family, your record, your usefulness, the fact that you have never done anything disgraceful. The question is not whether you have such things but whether any weight rests on them, and the honest test is what happens inside you when one is taken away.

What it does not mean. Paul was not anti-Jewish: he loved his people and could wish himself cut off for their sake (Romans 9:1–5). He opposed making circumcision a requirement for salvation, which turned grace into Christ plus something.

Who are the Judaizers today? Anyone who says Christ plus something is needed to be right with God. Today it is rarely circumcision, but a ritual, a church membership, rules about food, dress or days, a spiritual experience, a level of commitment, a list of good works. Any of these can be good in its place; made a condition of acceptance with God, or a badge of the real Christian, it changes the gospel. Watch for it in your own heart, where it is quieter and more dangerous. Finish this sentence honestly: “God accepts me because Christ died for me, and because I…” If anything comes after the “and”, that is where your confidence in the flesh is hiding. Bring it to God, set it down, and thank him that Christ is enough.

Is such harsh language ever right for Christians today? Rarely, and only in Paul’s kind of case. Jesus called the Pharisees “You serpents, you brood of vipers” (Matthew 23:33), and Paul uses strong words of those who corrupt the gospel (Galatians 5:12), but both reserve them for false teachers leading others away from salvation, not for honest doubters, ordinary opponents or weaker believers. The rule for ordinary correction is gentleness (2 Timothy 2:24–25). Sharpness has its place when the gospel itself is under attack, and even then it must not become contempt or the pleasure of a fight.

Where Christians differ: does we are the circumcision mean the church has replaced Israel? Some read it that way; others hold that Israel as a people still has a distinct future in God’s purposes. Paul means that all who worship by the Spirit and trust in Christ, Jew and Gentile alike, are the true people of God, the reality circumcision pointed to. He does not say here that the Jewish people have no further place in God’s purposes; elsewhere they are still beloved for the sake of their forefathers (Romans 11:28), and Christians differ on how that future will unfold. What is clear is that there is one people of God in Christ, and Jewish people are welcome in it, and need Christ to enter it, on the same terms as everyone else.

Textual note. The KJV’s worship God in the spirit follows later manuscripts; the earliest read by the Spirit of God.
verseByVerse.note: “Dogs” was a Jewish insult for Gentiles; Paul turns it on those insisting on circumcision. “Those who mutilate the flesh” (katatomē, a hacking) is a play on “the circumcision” (peritomē) in v. 3.

verseByVerse.quote: though I myself have reason for confidence in the flesh also. If anyone else thinks he has reason for confidence in the flesh, I have more: circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee; as to zeal, a persecutor of the church; as to righteousness under the law, blameless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone could have trusted his record before God, Paul could, and he had more to show than the teachers he is warning against.

Reason for confidence. Paul outranks the Judaizers on their own terms, so no one can say he rejects what he never had. Seven credentials follow: four inherited, three achieved.

Circumcised on the eighth day. The first four were his before he had any say: circumcised on the day the law required (Leviticus 12:3), not as an adult convert, but born into the covenant people of Israel.

The tribe of Benjamin. A real boast. Benjamin gave Israel her first king, Saul, whose name Paul carried, and alone stayed with Judah when the kingdom tore in two.

A Hebrew of Hebrews. Though born in the Greek city of Tarsus, he came of a family that had kept the language and the ways when it would have been easier to let them go.

A Pharisee. Then three achievements. The Pharisees were the strictest party (Acts 23:6; 26:5): not the sneering caricature, but the most rigorous and respected school in Judaism, devoted to obeying God in the detail.

A persecutor of the church. Offered as a credential: his zeal for God’s law drove him to persecute those he thought were betraying it (Acts 8:3; Galatians 1:13–14). On the old accounting his worst act was his best qualification.

Blameless. Not sinless, but by outward law-keeping, the record any neighbour could inspect, faultless. That is the horror of it: this man kept the rules impeccably and was a fierce enemy of the Son of God. Blamelessness had not made him good. It had made him dangerous. Yet Christ’s grace reached the man with the best record and the worst heart, and if it could remake Saul of Tarsus, no record is too good to need it, and none too bad to receive it.

The one blameless Israelite. Set Paul’s list beside his Lord. Jesus too was circumcised on the eighth day (Luke 2:21), born of Israel and under the law (Galatians 4:4), though of Judah (Hebrews 7:14). But his blamelessness went all the way in. He could ask his enemies, “Which one of you convicts me of sin?” (John 8:46), and no answer came. And where Saul’s zeal drove him to destroy others, Jesus’ zeal for his Father’s house cost him his own life (John 2:17). Paul can throw his own record away because there is a perfect one, and it belongs to the one in whom believers are found.

Is it wrong to be thankful for my Christian upbringing, my church or my heritage? Not at all. Paul lists Israel’s privileges with gratitude (Romans 9:4–5), and Timothy’s faith was first in his grandmother and mother (2 Timothy 1:5). A godly home and a faithful church are great gifts; the danger is only in trusting them. Thank God for them as means he used to bring you to Christ, and rest your confidence on Christ himself. A Christian heritage cannot save you, and the lack of one cannot keep you out.

Does this say anything to someone who is not religious? Yes, because everyone keeps a list. The irreligious version has different entries: I am decent, hardworking, honest, more tolerant than the religious people I know. Paul’s word flesh covers all of it: anything you offer as the reason you are acceptable. The moralist and the free spirit are both standing where Saul stood. The gospel says the same thing to each: the record that counts is not yours, and it is offered to you freely in Christ (v. 9).

Uncertain wording. “A Hebrew of Hebrews” is compressed. It certainly means a Hebrew born of Hebrew parents. Since Acts distinguishes Hebrews from Hellenists by language (Acts 6:1), it probably also means his family spoke Hebrew or Aramaic, though he was born abroad (compare Acts 22:2–3). Likely both: Hebrew by birth and by upbringing.
verseByVerse.note: Benjamin was the tribe of King Saul, Paul’s namesake. “Hebrew of Hebrews” may mean he was raised speaking Hebrew or Aramaic.

verseByVerse.quote: But whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of Christ. Indeed, I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. For his sake I have suffered the loss of all things and count them as rubbish, in order that I may gain Christ
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul moved everything he once counted as profit into the loss column, because knowing Christ is worth more than all of it.

Counted as loss. Paul speaks as a bookkeeper. “Gain” (kerdos) is profit, and “count” (hēgeomai) is the verb used of Christ, who “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped” (2:6). Paul does the same sum with his own assets. In verse 7 he “counted”, a decision made on the Damascus road and still standing; in verse 8 he says “I count”, in the present, and the list has widened to everything. Nearly thirty years on, this is no young convert’s enthusiasm.

The surpassing worth. Paul did not despise his old life and so turn to Christ. Everything on that list was real gain: the covenant, the law, the zeal. He met something beside which they could not hold their value. “Surpassing worth” (hyperechon) is worth that rises above everything else. Bring a lamp into a room at night and it is a genuine treasure; carry it outside at noon and you would put it down and forget it. Nothing has happened to the lamp.

My Lord. This singular, personal phrase about Christ appears almost nowhere else in his letters. Whatever else the Damascus road did, it left this man with a person he could call his own.

The loss of all things. Not only an accountant’s reckoning: Paul really lost status, career, friends, perhaps family, comfort and safety. The rising star of the Pharisees became a hunted itinerant who was beaten, stoned, shipwrecked and imprisoned (2 Corinthians 11:23–27).

Rubbish. Skybala is not a polite word, and “rubbish” is a polite translation: scraps thrown to the dogs, and, in its coarser use, dung. Paul has just called his opponents dogs; now his own pedigree belongs on the heap where they scavenge. Beside Christ, the most impressive religious record is garbage.

That I may gain Christ. Paul is like the man in Jesus’ parable who found treasure hidden in a field and in his joy sold all that he had and bought it (Matthew 13:44–46). That man is not grimly sacrificing. He is getting a bargain. And the wonder is that Christ counted us worth gaining: he, who had everything, gave up all things to make us his own.

Does counting everything as loss mean I should despise my family, my work or the good things of life? No. Paul counts them loss in comparison with Christ and as a ground of standing before God, not as worthless in themselves: everything created by God is good, to be received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4). The point is ranking, not rejecting. When Christ is first, every other good thing finds its proper place and is enjoyed more, not less, because it is no longer asked to carry the weight of a god. What must go is whatever competes with him.

How do I come to value Christ like this? Not by trying to despise other things, but by seeing more of him: the lamp is put down because the sun has risen. Look at Christ in the Gospels and the letters; ask God to open your eyes to his worth (Ephesians 1:17–18); sing about him; listen to believers who love him. Think back to the last time your career, your family name or your reputation as a sound Christian was threatened: did the loss feel like a lamp at noon, or the end of the world? If the second, you are not disqualified; you have been shown where to look. People often discover his worth most deeply when they lose something precious and find him still there. Tell Christ today what he is worth to you, and ask him to make it truer.

verseByVerse.quote: and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends on faith—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s whole hope before God is to be found in Christ, clothed in a righteousness God gives through faith, not one he has made. This verse is the doctrinal centre of the letter.

And be found in him. Found on the day of Christ, the day this letter keeps returning to (1:6, 10; 2:16). Paul pictures the final judgment, and his whole hope is to be found inside someone else: not beside Christ with his own record in his hand, but in him. Faith joins a believer to Christ so closely that what belongs to Christ is counted as his: Christ’s death for sin, and Christ’s obedience, which becomes his righteousness (Romans 6:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

A righteousness of my own. Two kinds of righteousness, or right standing before God. The first is “my own”, produced by my law-keeping and effort, and the crucial word is “own”. Paul’s law-keeping did not fall a little short; outwardly he was blameless. He does not want it at all. It is the wrong kind of thing, like a forged coin, refused however much of it you bring. And it has only two results, both fatal: if you think you have achieved it, pride, and in Paul pride produced a persecutor; if you know you have not, despair.

Through faith in Christ. The other righteousness is received, not achieved (on the wording, see the box below).

The righteousness from God. From God (ek theou), not from me: God’s gift, credited to believers (Romans 3:21–22). This is what the Reformers meant by imputation: a righteousness not produced in me but credited to me, Christ’s record entered in my account because I am in him. Luther called it an alien righteousness, one from outside us, and that is its comfort. What we could never produce, God gives; what we could never earn, he credits; and the one who is found in Christ is found clothed in the spotless obedience of the Son of God.

The empty hand. Faith earns nothing; a beggar’s open palm does not buy the bread, it takes it. So assurance is possible. If my standing rested on a righteousness of my own, every bad week would move the ground under me. Because it rests on his, my standing on my worst day is exactly what it was on my best, and will be on the day I am found in him. Even a believer’s best works, still mixed with sin, are accepted only because they are offered in him (1 Peter 2:5). And only now does verse 10 make sense: Paul wants to know Christ and share his sufferings not in order to be accepted, but because he already is. This is the gospel the Philippians are to stand firm in (1:27), and the reason the joy of 3:1 cannot be taken from them.

If I am clothed in Christ’s righteousness, why does my sin still matter? Because you belong to the one whose righteousness you wear. Sin no longer threatens your standing, but it grieves your Father, harms you and others, and contradicts who you now are, and God disciplines his children not to make them pay but to make them share his holiness (Hebrews 12:10). A person who truly rests in Christ’s righteousness will want to be like him; a faith content to go on in sin has not understood what it was given (Romans 6:1–2). Confess your sins honestly, knowing that confession does not earn your acceptance but enjoys it.

Is it fair for God to count guilty people righteous? Not if it were make-believe: a judge who declared a guilty man innocent would be corrupt (Proverbs 17:15). But God does not pretend. The penalty for the sins of those in Christ was really paid at the cross, and the obedience credited to them was really lived by Christ, every day of his life. Because believers are joined to him, his record becomes theirs as truly as their sin became his (2 Corinthians 5:21). So God is shown to be just, and also the one who justifies everyone who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). Justification is not God lowering the standard. It is God meeting it himself.

Where Christians differ: whose righteousness? Some scholars of the New Perspective on Paul (a modern school that reads Paul’s debates as chiefly about the marks of Jewish identity) say the righteousness of my own that comes from the law means only Jewish identity, the privileges of belonging to Israel, and that the righteousness from God means God’s own covenant faithfulness, or covenant membership, rather than a righteous status credited to the believer. They rightly stress that the gospel makes Jew and Gentile one people. This commentary’s view: this verse is one of the clearest in Scripture on imputed righteousness. Paul’s list in vv. 5–6 does include his Jewish credentials, but also his zeal and his blamelessness under the law, and he sets all of it against a righteousness that is God’s gift. He contrasts a righteousness of my own, from the law, with a righteousness from God, through faith: a status given by God, not produced by us, received by faith. This is justification by the imputed righteousness of Christ (Romans 4:5–6; the Westminster Confession 11.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 11.1). Covenant membership follows, but the heart is a righteous standing before the Judge.

Uncertain wording. The Greek behind “faith in Christ” (pistis Christou) can mean either faith in Christ or the faithfulness of Christ, and the ESV note mentions the second. Faith in Christ, our trust in him, is the better reading, as in Galatians 2:16, since the verse goes on to say this righteousness “depends on faith”. Either way the gospel is the same: Christ’s faithful obedience is the righteousness, and our faith receives it.

verseByVerse.quote: that I may know him and the power of his resurrection, and may share his sufferings, becoming like him in his death,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s deepest desire is to know Christ himself, both in the power of his resurrection and in the fellowship of his sufferings, being shaped into the pattern of his death.

That I may know him. Everything has been building to this. Not to know about him, nor even his benefits: him. The verb (ginōskō) means personal knowledge, the word for Adam knowing his wife, and for God’s “You only have I known” (Amos 3:2): the knowing that happens between persons. The man who had seen the risen Lord and been caught up to the third heaven writes as though he were still at the beginning. Few have known Christ better, and nobody wanted to know him more.

The power of his resurrection. The power that raised Christ is at work in believers now: new life, victory over sin, strength in weakness (Ephesians 1:19–20; Romans 6:4). It is named before suffering, the reverse of Christ’s own story, because you meet the risen Lord first, and only his power makes it possible to walk into suffering at all.

Share his sufferings. “Share” means fellowship (koinōnia), the partnership word of chapter 1. Fellowship with Christ includes fellowship in suffering for his sake (Romans 8:17; 1 Peter 4:13). Our sufferings do not pay for sin, as his did; we walk the path he walked.

Becoming like him in his death. “Becoming like” is one word meaning conformed to (symmorphizomenos), and inside it is the word of 2:6–7 for the form of God and the form of a servant (morphē). Paul is being pressed into the shape of the one who poured himself out, now, in a cell awaiting a verdict: dying to self daily (2 Corinthians 4:10–11), and perhaps dying as a martyr. He regards the suffering not as the price of the power but as part of the prize, because the person he wants to know went to a cross. And Christ went into death so that his people would never meet death without him, and rose so that the road through death would end in resurrection.

Why would anyone long for this? Most of us do not, and Paul was not asking for pain for its own sake. Five things explain it.

1. The goal is Christ, not the pain. A wife who spends nights at her husband’s hospital bed does not long for hospitals; she longs to be with him, and that is where he is. Love wants to share the beloved’s life, the hard parts too (Ruth 1:16), and Paul would not leave out the part of Christ’s life that was the cross.

2. In this life the power and the suffering come together. My power is made perfect in weakness, the Lord told him (2 Corinthians 12:9). He carried the death of Jesus in his body so that the life of Jesus might be shown in it (2 Corinthians 4:7–11), and when everyone deserted him at his trial, the Lord stood by him (2 Timothy 4:16–17). The times he suffered for Christ were the times he knew Christ nearest.

3. Suffering for Christ marks you as his. The world treats his followers as it treated him (John 15:18–20). The apostles left the council rejoicing to be counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (Acts 5:41), and suffering for Christ has been granted to the Philippians as a gift, alongside faith (1:29).

4. The road leads to glory. Christ went through the cross to the resurrection, and his people follow (v. 11): we suffer with him in order to be glorified with him (Romans 8:17). Paul weighed it and called it light, momentary affliction beside an eternal weight of glory (2 Corinthians 4:17).

5. Paul was in prison as he wrote. No wish from an armchair: in chains, facing possible death (1:20–23), he is saying, I would rather have Christ with chains than comfort without him.

What it does not mean. Not seeking suffering, enjoying pain, or inflicting it on yourself. Paul begged three times for his thorn to be removed (2 Corinthians 12:8), and Jesus prayed that the cup might pass (Matthew 26:39). It means accepting suffering, when it comes in Christ’s service, as part of knowing him. Nor are you a poor Christian if you do not feel this longing: start by asking to know Christ, and the willingness grows as love grows.

What “dying to self” actually means. Not a biblical phrase, but it sums up Luke 9:23 (deny yourself and take up your cross daily) and Galatians 2:20 (I have been crucified with Christ). It has three parts.

1. Something that has already happened. If you trust Christ, your old self, ruled by sin, was crucified with him (Romans 6:6): a fact to believe and live out (Romans 6:11). Sin is no longer your master, even when it still shouts.

2. Something you do every day. The self that wants the throne still fights, so each day you say no to it: to my will above God’s, my comfort above another’s good, my reputation above the truth. You bite back the cutting reply; you admit you were wrong, without excuses; you give up your Saturday to help someone move house; you turn down the deal that would mean bending the truth; you put to death the sins Paul names (Colossians 3:5–9).

3. Always for the sake of life. The grain dies to bear much fruit (John 12:24); by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, and live (Romans 8:13). What dies is selfishness and sin; what lives is the real you, made new and becoming like Christ.

What dying to self does not mean. Not erasing your personality: Paul stayed recognisably Paul, blunt, warm and learned. Not self-hatred: the verse that says I have been crucified with Christ goes on, who loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20), so you die to self as someone deeply loved.

Not being a doormat. You may say no and have needs, and you must not let others use or abuse you. Jesus withdrew from the crowds to rest and pray (Mark 6:31). Dying to self is death to sin and selfishness, not to wisdom, boundaries or protecting the vulnerable.

Not neglecting or punishing your body. Harsh treatment of the body does not stop the indulgence of the flesh (Colossians 2:20–23); rest, food, sleep and medical care are not selfishness. Nor is it done in your own strength, but by the Spirit (Romans 8:13). And it is not the loss of joy: whoever loses his life for Christ’s sake will find it (Matthew 16:25). The aim is a fuller life, not a smaller one.

How do I actually get to know Christ better? As you know any person: by time with him and listening to him. Read the Gospels slowly, asking what each scene shows you about him. Pray, not only with requests: tell him what you love about him. Come to the Lord’s Table, where he gives himself to be received by faith. Obey him, for he shows himself to those who keep his word (John 14:21). Spend time with Christians who know him well. And do not waste hard times in following him: ask to meet him there, where Paul knew him nearest. Pray Paul’s prayer this morning: Lord, let me know you, the power of your resurrection, and the fellowship of your sufferings. Then choose one ordinary way to die to self today, not to prove anything, but because you belong to the one who died for you.

verseByVerse.quote: that by any means possible I may attain the resurrection from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is sure of the destination, the resurrection to glory, and open about the road by which God will bring him there. “By any means possible” is humility about the way, not doubt about the end.

That by any means possible. Literally, “if somehow”. Is Paul unsure, after the confidence of 1:6? This is the man for whom “to die is gain” (1:21), and in the next verse Christ has already made him his own. He means: whatever it takes, however God chooses to bring me there, through suffering and death if need be. He does not know whether he arrives by a Roman sword or an old man’s bed. He is attached not to the road but to the destination.

Certain, but not casual. God will keep you, and you must press on. The Paul who wrote that he who began a good work will bring it to completion also wrote, “But I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified” (1 Corinthians 9:27). The certainty never produces a shrug.

Attain the resurrection. “Attain” (katantaō) is to arrive at the destination: the bodily resurrection of the righteous at Christ’s return (1 Corinthians 15:23). Literally it is the “out-resurrection” from among the dead: not merely the raising of all people, which the wicked share (John 5:28–29), but the resurrection to glory, this lowly body remade like Christ’s (v. 21).

Raised from the dead first. Paul’s words for his goal, resurrection from the dead, are the words the New Testament uses of Easter: Christ was raised from the dead, never to die again (Romans 6:9), the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18). Paul hopes to arrive where his Lord already is, by the road his Lord took. That is why “if somehow” does not shake him: the resurrection he reaches for has already happened once, to the man who met him on the Damascus road, and the resurrection of every believer is joined to that one as the harvest to its first sheaf (1 Corinthians 15:20–23).

Does the out-resurrection mean believers are raised at a different time from everyone else? Some read it as a first resurrection of believers separated from a later one. Premillennial Christians, who expect Christ to reign on earth for a thousand years between two resurrections (Revelation 20:4–6), are faithful brothers and sisters who love the same returning Lord. But the phrase describes the character of the resurrection, not a separate timetable. Jesus speaks of one hour in which all who are in the tombs hear his voice, the righteous and the unrighteous (John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15), and then the judgment: for believers a resurrection to glory, for others to judgment. Paul is longing for the glorious side of that one great day, not for an earlier event.

What if I am unsure whether I will make it? Christians sometimes fear that any uncertainty proves their faith counterfeit. But a man utterly sure of his destination can write a cautious line about the road, because the caution concerns not God’s faithfulness but what the next year holds. Not knowing what is coming is not the same as doubting who is waiting. Your assurance rests on Christ’s promise and work, not on your ability to foresee the road (John 10:28). Keep looking to him, keep pressing on, and trust him to bring you there.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–16 — Not Arrived, and Still Running
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Belonging to Christ is not the same as having arrived, and knowing the difference is what maturity is. Paul has not reached perfection, but presses on to take hold of the goal because Christ has already taken hold of him; forgetting what lies behind, he runs toward the prize of God’s upward call (vv. 12–14). Mature believers think the same way; where they differ, God will make things clear, and meanwhile they live by what they have already reached (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Sanctification Is Progress, Not Arrival

Holiness in this life is real but incomplete. Verse 12 is the apostle’s own testimony to that, and its order drives the Christian life (see the note on vv. 12–14); on the paradox of maturity, see vv. 15–16.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Some in the early church claimed to be spiritually complete already, and Paul’s denial corrects them. Where believers still differ, he leaves it to God to persuade them.

verseByVerse.quote: Not that I have already obtained this or am already perfect, but I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own. Brothers, I do not consider that I have made it my own. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has not yet arrived, so he runs with everything he has toward the finish, because Christ has already taken hold of him.

Not already perfect. After such lofty sentences Paul guards against misunderstanding. “Perfect” (teleioō) means complete, brought to the goal, and he has not reached full conformity to Christ. Every century has had those who taught a settled plateau where the striving is over, perhaps some in Philippi too. Paul, who had more right than anyone to claim it, refuses.

Christ has made me his own. “Press on” (diōkō) is to pursue, to chase, the word used of his persecuting the church in verse 6: the same energy, now redirected. And “make it my own” (katalambanō) is to seize, used of both Paul and Christ. Paul is chasing Christ because Christ has already caught him, on the Damascus road, travelling the other way with arrest warrants in his bag. Grace comes first; effort follows. Running in order to be accepted is exhausting and never finished; Paul runs because he already belongs, so he can admit he has not arrived without being crushed.

One thing I do. First honesty (“I do not consider that I have made it my own”), then a single aim. A man with a dozen churches on his conscience and a trial pending says his life has one thing in it.

Forgetting what lies behind. Not amnesia: Paul has just listed his past. It means refusing to let the past rule, through boasting or despair. He had blood on his hands and could have spent his life punishing himself for it; he must also forget his successes, which is harder and less often preached. A runner glancing back at either is losing the race.

Straining forward. “Straining forward” (epekteinomai) is stretching out toward: a runner whose chest reaches the line ahead of his legs.

The goal and the prize. “Goal” (skopos) is the mark, the target the eye is fixed on. “Prize” (brabeion) is the victor’s wreath at the games (1 Corinthians 9:24). The prize is Christ himself, and eternal glory with him: not a trophy God hands over, but God calling his runner home.

The runner is already held. The perfection Paul lacks has already been supplied: Christ obeyed perfectly in his place, and that obedience, not the quality of his running, is what he is found in (3:9). Every stumble in the race is real, and none of them can undo his standing.

How do I forget what lies behind when my past is terrible, or when I was badly hurt? Forgetting does not mean pretending it did not happen, nor that wrongs done to you must never be named or brought to justice. It means the past no longer steers. If your past is your sin, it has been nailed to the cross; confess anything unconfessed, make what amends you can, and then refuse to keep paying for what Christ has paid for. If your past is what others did to you, bring it to God, get help to heal, seek justice where that is right, and ask him for the grace to forgive. Healing may take a long time. But your future is defined by the upward call of God, not by what happened behind you.

What if I feel I am barely running at all? The race is long, and runners have bad stretches; Paul himself had not arrived. What matters is the direction you face and that you keep getting up, running because you are held, not to get held. Lean on other runners; the Christian race is never a solo event (Hebrews 12:1–2). And fix your eyes on Jesus, the founder and perfecter of faith, who ran ahead of you and is waiting at the line.

Where Christians differ: Christian perfection. Some traditions, notably Wesleyan and Holiness churches, teach that believers can attain sinless perfection or entire sanctification, a settled state of perfect love, in this life; they rightly long for holiness and will not settle for less. This commentary’s view: Paul, late in his ministry, says he is not yet perfect and still pressing on. Believers grow in holiness, but perfection comes only at glorification (1 John 1:8; 3:2; the Westminster Confession 13.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 13.2). The Christian life is a race to the end, not a plateau. Sanctification is the Spirit’s lifelong work of making a believer actually holy in heart and life; glorification is God’s finishing of that work, begun when a believer dies and goes to be with Christ and completed at the resurrection, when sin is gone for ever (Romans 8:30; Hebrews 12:23).

Uncertain wording. “The upward call” is literally “the call above”: either God’s call from heaven that set Paul running, or the summons to come up at the end, perhaps as winners at the games were called up by the herald. The phrase allows both, and they belong together: the God who called him at the start calls him home at the finish.
verseByVerse.note: The picture is of a runner straining toward the finishing line.

verseByVerse.quote: Let those of us who are mature think this way, and if in anything you think otherwise, God will reveal that also to you. Only let us hold true to what we have attained.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mature believers know they have not arrived; where they still see differently, God will teach them, and meanwhile they live by the truth they already have.

Those who are mature. Mature (teleioi) is the same root as “perfect” in verse 12, which Paul said he was not. Three verses after denying he is perfect, he wryly counts himself among the mature, and that is the lesson. Maturity is not having arrived; maturity is knowing you have not.

God will reveal that also. A gracious sentence about disagreement. The apostle who called his opponents dogs does not press here, but trusts God to correct believers on secondary matters as they grow. This is patience, not indifference: he plainly thinks he is right, and is sure enough of the truth to let God do the persuading.

Knowing which question is in front of you. On the gospel itself, whether righteousness comes by law or by faith, Paul gives no ground; there the language is dogs and mutilators. On how the life of pressing on works out, where sincere Christians differ, he is patient. Knowing which question is in front of you is most of pastoral wisdom. Treat every disagreement as a first-order matter (one the gospel depends on) and you will tear a congregation apart; treat none of them as first-order and you will lose the gospel.

Hold true. Then what everyone must do meanwhile. “Hold true” (stoicheō) is a marching word: keep in line, walk in step with. Whatever remains unresolved, live up to the truth you already know. You do not have to solve everything before you obey anything.

The mind that does not grasp. “Think this way” (phroneō) is the word of 2:5, where Paul tells the church to have among themselves the mind that is theirs in Christ Jesus. The Son, who was equal with God, did not cling to his rights; the mature believer does not claim to have arrived. And the promise that God will reveal is a promise about the Son. It is the Father’s delight to show his Son to those humble enough to be taught as little children (Matthew 11:25–27), and the Spirit whom Christ sent guides his people into the truth (John 16:13).

How do I tell a gospel issue from a secondary one? Ask whether it touches how a sinner is made right with God, who Christ is, or the authority of Scripture. Those are first-order, with no compromise: the deity and humanity of Christ, his atoning death and bodily resurrection, justification by grace through faith, the Trinity. Many other matters, such as details of church practice, views of the end times, or conscience about food and days, are worth discussing, but sincere believers differ on them and remain brothers. Hold your convictions firmly there too, but hold your brothers more firmly.

What should I do when I think a fellow believer is wrong on such a matter? Pray for them before you talk to them. Speak humbly, from Scripture, and listen as well as argue; you may be the one who needs correcting. Then leave the persuading to God and keep walking in step together, without making it a test of fellowship, campaigning or gossiping. And look to your own obedience first: are you living up to what you already know?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–21 — Two Ways to Walk, and Where You Are From
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Where you belong decides how you walk. Paul invites the church to follow his example and that of others who live the same way (v. 17), because many, he says with tears, live as enemies of the cross, ruled by appetite and heading for ruin (vv. 18–19). Believers are citizens of heaven, waiting for a Saviour from there, the Lord Jesus Christ (v. 20), and by the power with which he rules all things he will transform their weak and humble bodies to be like his glorious body (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology:
Citizenship, and a Body That Will Be Raised

The citizenship of verse 20 (politeuma) is not a picture of escape (see the note on v. 20). Verse 21 completes the pattern of the hymn in chapter 2 and applies it to us: our lowly body will be changed, not discarded (see the note on v. 21).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: “Join in imitating me” was said to people with no New Testament and no Christian upbringing (on why it was not arrogance, see the note on vv. 17–19).

Now: For the one who is ill, or ageing, or watching a body they love fail, see the note on v. 21.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, join in imitating me, and keep your eyes on those who walk according to the example you have in us. For many, of whom I have often told you and now tell you even with tears, walk as enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and they glory in their shame, with minds set on earthly things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Follow those whose lives are shaped by the cross, and weep over those who live for their appetites, for their road ends in ruin.

Join in imitating me. “Join in imitating” (symmimētai) means be fellow imitators. Is that arrogance? No, for three reasons. Paul always means “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1): a signpost, not the destination. These Christians had no New Testament, and many were barely a decade out of paganism; the gospel had to be seen before it could be copied, and they had seen it in a man beaten with rods in their own city and singing hymns at midnight in the cell (Acts 16:22–25). And five verses earlier he said he was not yet perfect, which is what makes him safe to follow.

Keep your eyes on them. “Keep your eyes on” (skopeō) shares its root with the goal of verse 14. And not on Paul only: any life running toward that goal will do. Somewhere in your own congregation there is a quiet old saint worth watching more closely than you have.

Even with tears. Paul’s composure breaks, and that is the tone to hold on to. He is not sneering or enjoying the denunciation; tears are the right posture from which to describe another person’s ruin. Christ wept over Jerusalem, and his apostle wept over the enemies of the cross, because the heart of God does not delight in the destruction of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11).

Enemies of the cross. Paul does not say who they are; probably they professed faith while living for themselves, perhaps treating grace as permission to sin. He describes them by how they lived. The cross is the pattern of chapter 2, self-emptying for the interests of others, and a life organised around self-indulgence contradicts it whatever it professes on a Sunday.

Their end is destruction. Four marks follow, and Paul names where the road ends before he describes it. “Destruction” (apōleia, as in 1:28) is eternal ruin, and Paul does not soften it, because God is holy: a life ruled by appetite ends where every rival god ends, under his judgment, shut out from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:9).

Their god is their belly. Appetite in the place of worship: food, sex, comfort, pleasure (Romans 16:18). Whatever in you says “I want” has been put on the throne, and it is a god that must be fed daily and never says thank you.

They glory in their shame. Their boasting is upside down: the very things that should have made them hide are the things they advertise.

Minds set on earthly things. The root of it all. “Minds set” is phroneō, the letter’s key word, the opposite of the mind of Christ (2:5). It is the quietest diagnosis and the most searching, describing not an act but the direction of a life: where the mind settles when nothing is demanding its attention, what you think about in the ten minutes before sleep. That is what Paul is weeping over, and it is far more ordinary than the phrase “enemies of the cross” leads us to expect.

In the flow. The chapter began with people who trusted the flesh by adding rules to Christ (vv. 2–3), and it ends with people who serve the flesh by indulging it. Both miss the cross from opposite directions, one by adding to it and the other by ignoring it, and Christ’s people are to follow neither.

He despised the shame. Set the four marks against the cross, and each is reversed in Christ. Their end is destruction; his death rescues from destruction all who trust him. Their god is their belly; he was hungry in the wilderness and still refused to make his appetite his master (Matthew 4:2–4). They glory in their shame; he endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2), and bore a disgrace that was ours so that his people might share his glory. Their minds are set on earthly things; his mind is the mind of 2:5, set on the Father’s will and the good of others. An enemy of the cross is the exact opposite of the crucified Christ.

A shameless age, and a deeply ashamed one. Our culture thinks it has finished with shame: what earlier generations hid, we post. Yet few cultures have been so soaked in it: ashamed of our bodies, our incomes, an old remark dug up online, of not being as happy as everyone else looks. Shame has not gone away; it has moved. We glory in what God calls shameful and are crushed by what he does not care about at all, and Paul’s phrase catches both halves. The gospel does not bring back the old respectable shame, which only drove sinners into hiding. It answers with a cross, where the Son of God was stripped and mocked in public so that those who come to him might be covered and honoured by God himself. People whom God has clothed no longer need either to flaunt or to hide.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians cannot enjoy food or earthly gifts. God richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17). It means those gifts must not become gods.

Can a true Christian be an enemy of the cross? A true believer can fall into serious sin for a time, as David and Peter did, and must be called to repent. But Paul describes a settled way of life, and those who live that way, whatever they profess, show that they do not belong to Christ (1 John 3:6–10). That is why Paul weeps rather than shrugs. If you are troubled by this, the trouble is a good sign; enemies of the cross do not grieve over their sin. Turn to Christ now, and keep turning.

What if the people I look up to let me down? Some will; every human model is flawed, which is why Paul points through himself to Christ. Choose models whose lives are cross-shaped, not merely gifted or successful, and watch how they handle failure. When a model falls, grieve, learn, and do not let it shake your faith in the one they were pointing to. And remember that you are someone’s model too.

verseByVerse.quote: But our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers belong to heaven and live here as its citizens, eagerly waiting for their Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, to come from there.

But our citizenship is in heaven. “But” is the hinge, turning from minds set on earthly things. The noun is politeuma, commonwealth, homeland, related to the verb Paul used in 1:27 when he told them to live as citizens worthy of the gospel. A politeuma was a body of citizens resident in a foreign place, holding the rights and duties of a homeland they might never have seen.

Living in one place, belonging to another. Philippi was a Roman colony, settled with discharged legionaries and governed by Roman law (see the introduction). Its people were intensely proud of their Roman citizenship; Paul had been charged there with advocating customs “not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice” (Acts 16:21). Paul takes the proudest fact about their city as a picture of something truer: your capital is not Rome. The church is a colony of heaven on earth.

Not evacuation. Citizenship in heaven is not escape from the world or permission to stop caring about it. A Roman colony was not homesick settlers waiting for a boat; it was Rome made visible on the frontier, and that is what the church is in Philippi for.

We await a Saviour. The verb (apekdechomai) is eager, expectant waiting, as in Romans 8:19–25. Saviour (sōtēr) and lord (kyrios) were both titles claimed by Caesar. In a colony of Caesar’s veterans, Paul says quietly that the Saviour and Lord is someone else.

The Lord Jesus Christ. He will come from heaven, as an emperor might visit a colony to rescue it. Christ has a commonwealth that no army can conquer and no time can wear out, and he has made us its citizens by his blood. The question is not whether you believe he is coming, but whether anything in the way you live this week would only make sense if he were.

Should Christians care about their country, vote or serve in public life? Yes, but as citizens of heaven first. Paul used his Roman citizenship when it served the gospel (Acts 16:37; 22:25), and told Christians to pray for those in authority and seek the good of their society (1 Timothy 2:1–2; Romans 13:1–7). Love your neighbour, work for justice, vote with a conscience shaped by Scripture, and serve where you are called. But do not put your ultimate hope in any party, leader or nation, and do not let earthly loyalties outrank Christ. When the two conflict, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29).

Will we live in heaven for ever? Believers who die go to be with Christ there (1:23), but the final hope is not a disembodied existence. Christ will come from heaven, raise the dead, and make all things new: a new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1–4). The capital comes down to the colony. God will dwell with his people, in resurrected bodies, in a renewed creation, for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Philippi’s citizens were proud to be citizens of Rome; believers belong to a heavenly commonwealth.

verseByVerse.quote: who will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body, by the power that enables him even to subject all things to himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Christ comes, he will change our weak and dying bodies to be like his own glorious body, by the power with which he rules all things. The hymn of chapter 2 is now applied to us: as Christ was humbled and exalted, so will his people be.

Our lowly body. “Transform” (metaschēmatizō) is to change the form, the outward state. “Our lowly body” is literally the body of our humiliation, and the noun comes from the same root as “he humbled himself” in 2:8. Everyone over forty knows it: these bodies are weak, ageing, sick and dying (2 Corinthians 4:16; 5:4), and anyone who has watched a strong parent become unable to manage a staircase knows Paul has not exaggerated.

Like his glorious body. “Like” means conformed (symmorphos), built again on the word for form (morphē), the root of “the form of God” in 2:6 and “becoming like him in his death” in verse 10. The pattern is complete: he took our form so that we might share his. The resurrection body will be like Christ’s risen body: imperishable, glorious, powerful (1 Corinthians 15:42–44; 1 John 3:2).

Transformation, not escape. Much Greek thought around Philippi held that salvation meant the soul getting free of the body. Paul says the body will be changed: the same body, made glorious, as Christ’s risen body was recognisably his own, still bearing the marks of the nails (John 20:27), and yet transfigured.

The power to subject all things. The guarantee: the power that will bring the whole created order under Christ’s feet, death included (Psalm 8:6; 1 Corinthians 15:27), will be applied to your body.

He carried our nature up into glory. Christ wore the body of humiliation before we did. He was weary at a well, wept at a grave, was scourged and crucified and laid in another man’s tomb, and on the third day that same body came out glorious. He did not leave our frailty behind when he rose; he carried our nature up into glory, and from the throne he will reach down with the power that rules all things and lift every one of his people out of the dust. The aged, the broken and the buried will rise in his likeness, and the eyes that closed in death will open on his face.

Where the chapter has been going. Paul opened by throwing his pedigree out with the kitchen refuse and closes with the humiliated body made glorious. That is why minds must not be set on earthly things: not because earthly things are unreal, but because they are not where the story is going.

Neither idol nor machine. Our culture is oddly divided about the body. It is almost worshipped, trained, tracked, sculpted and photographed, as though a well-kept body proved a well-kept life; and it is treated as hardware the real me merely uses, to be modified at will, or one day left behind by copying the mind into a machine. The first is the belly-worship of verse 19; the second is the old Greek dream of escaping the flesh. Christianity has always seemed too bodily to the sophisticated; the second-century critic Celsus sneered that the resurrection was a hope fit for worms. But its God made matter and called it good, took a body himself, and kept it after Easter. So the Christian cannot idolise the body, since it is lowly and must be changed, and cannot despise it, since it is the very thing Christ means to raise. You are not a ghost driving a machine. You are a creature he intends to bring, whole, into glory.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we will become divine. We will be glorified humans, like Christ in his humanity, never sharing his deity.

What about bodies that were destroyed, cremated or lost at sea? The resurrection does not depend on the condition of the remains. The God who made the first body from the dust can raise it from any dust, and his power is not limited by fire, sea or decay (Revelation 20:13). Christians may differ on burial and cremation as a matter of practice and witness, but no believer’s resurrection is in any doubt because of how their body was laid to rest.

What does this mean for someone who is disabled, ill or ageing? Your present weakness is not the last word about you. The body of humiliation will be raised in power and glory, free from pain, disease and decay. That does not make present suffering small, and you are free to grieve it and seek every help now. But you may also hope, concretely and bodily. Many disabled believers have said that the first face they will see with perfect eyes, and the first steps they take on perfect legs, will be towards Christ. The New Testament does not tell you the body does not matter. It tells you the body matters so much that God intends to raise it.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. To write the same things to you is no trouble to me and is safe for you.<sup>2</sup>Look out for the dogs, look out for the evildoers, look out for those who mutilate the flesh.<sup>3</sup>For we are the circumcision, who worship by the Spirit of God and glory in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh—<sup>4</sup>though I myself have reason for confidence in the flesh also. If anyone else thinks he has reason for confidence in the flesh, I have more:<sup>5</sup>circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee;<sup>6</sup>as to zeal, a persecutor of the church; as to righteousness under the law, blameless.<sup>7</sup>But whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of Christ.<sup>8</sup>Indeed, I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. For his sake I have suffered the loss of all things and count them as rubbish, in order that I may gain Christ<sup>9</sup>and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends on faith—<sup>10</sup>that I may know him and the power of his resurrection, and may share his sufferings, becoming like him in his death,<sup>11</sup>that by any means possible I may attain the resurrection from the dead.<sup>12</sup>Not that I have already obtained this or am already perfect, but I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own.<sup>13</sup>Brothers, I do not consider that I have made it my own. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead,<sup>14</sup>I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.<sup>15</sup>Let those of us who are mature think this way, and if in anything you think otherwise, God will reveal that also to you.<sup>16</sup>Only let us hold true to what we have attained.<sup>17</sup>Brothers, join in imitating me, and keep your eyes on those who walk according to the example you have in us.<sup>18</sup>For many, of whom I have often told you and now tell you even with tears, walk as enemies of the cross of Christ.<sup>19</sup>Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and they glory in their shame, with minds set on earthly things.<sup>20</sup>But our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ,<sup>21</sup>who will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body, by the power that enables him even to subject all things to himself.

keyVerse.quote: Indeed, I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord.
keyVerse.note: This is the chapter’s verdict in Paul’s own words. Everything before it, his pedigree and his record, goes into the loss column because of it, and everything after it, the righteousness that comes through faith, the longing to share Christ’s sufferings and the race toward the prize, unpacks what knowing him means. It also names a person, not a principle: “my Lord”, the one who made Paul his own.

3.reflection:
Paul says the true people of God “put no confidence in the flesh” (v. 3). Finish the sentence honestly: “God accepts me because Christ died for me, and because I…” What tends to come after the “and” for you, and why is it so hard to set down?

Paul did not despise his heritage and record; he found something beside which they lost their value, like a lamp at noon (vv. 7–8). What good things in your life are most likely to compete with Christ, and how would ranking him first change the way you enjoy them?

Paul runs hard because Christ has already made him his own (v. 12), and he forgets both his failures and his successes (v. 13). Which part of your past most often pulls your eyes backwards, and how does belonging to Christ free you from it?

Our citizenship is in heaven, and we await a Saviour who will transform our lowly bodies (vv. 20–21). What in the way you live this week would only make sense if he is really coming, and how does this hope speak to someone you know who is ill, ageing or grieving?

4.title: The Peace That Passes Understanding: Rejoice, Pray, and Be Content
4.overview:
Where we are. The last chapter turns the letter into practice. Its “therefore” reaches back to 3:20–21, the citizens of heaven awaiting their Saviour.

The message. The Lord is near, and he is enough. Because he is near, his people can stand firm, make peace with one another, rejoice, let go of their rights and bring every worry to God, and his peace will guard their hearts. Because Christ strengthens them, they can be content with little or with much, for the God who supplies every need in Christ Jesus is the real treasure, not the gift.

Why it was said. The church in Philippi was poor, opposed and anxious for its imprisoned apostle, and two of its leading women had fallen out (see the introduction). It had also sent Paul a costly gift, and he needed to thank them without seeming to ask for more or to lean on them more than on Christ.

How the chapter makes its case. Paul urges the church to stand firm and pleads with Euodia and Syntyche to agree in the Lord, asking a trusted helper to bring them together (vv. 1–3). Short commands follow for a church under strain: rejoice, be gentle, pray instead of worrying, fill the mind with what is true and lovely, practise what you saw in Paul, with the promise first of God’s peace and then of the God of peace himself (vv. 4–9). Finally he thanks them for their gift without depending on it: he has learned contentment through Christ, treasures their partnership, calls the gift a fragrant sacrifice, and promises that God will supply every need of theirs, before closing with praise, greetings and grace (vv. 10–23).

Where it leads. The chapter keeps arriving at Christ. The quarrelling women are written in the book of life of the Lamb slain for them both. The peace that guards the anxious is the peace Jesus left his disciples the night before he died. The strength that makes a prisoner content comes from the one who had nowhere to lay his head. The gift that rose to God like incense is a small copy of Christ’s offering of himself, and every need is met from riches stored up in him. The letter that opened with grace ends with “the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ” (v. 23).

For us. This chapter does not shame the anxious, the discontented or the quarrelling; it shows them where to go. Name the quarrel you need to end, the worry you need to hand over and the thing you think you cannot be content without, and bring each one to the Lord who is near.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Stand Firm, and Two Women Who Cannot Agree
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A church that is to stand firm against the world must first be at peace within. Paul urges the believers he loves to hold their ground in the Lord, as citizens of heaven awaiting their Saviour (v. 1). Then he names the seam where the line could break: two women who laboured beside him in the gospel have fallen out. He pleads with each of them alike to agree in the Lord, asks a trusted companion to help them, and reminds the church that their names, like those of all his fellow workers, are written in the book of life (vv. 2–3).
verseByVerse.theology:
What Christian Unity Rests On

The appeal to these two women shows the ground of unity: not agreement on every point but a shared life in Christ, one Lord, one Spirit, one book of life. A congregation whose unity rests on everyone agreeing will fracture at the first serious disagreement; one whose unity rests on Christ can carry real friction without breaking.

Paul does not judge between them, and he ends with God’s choice of them (see the note on vv. 2–3).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: These were not marginal figures. The Philippian church had begun among women at a riverside prayer meeting (Acts 16:13), so these two women had very likely belonged to it from its first days.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my brothers, whom I love and long for, my joy and crown, stand firm thus in the Lord, my beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because your future in Christ is certain, hold your ground in him together, as people deeply loved. Paul wraps a single command, stand firm, in more affection than almost any other verse he wrote.

Therefore. The word reaches back to 3:20–21: our citizenship is in heaven, and Christ will transform our bodies by the power that subjects all things to himself. The command to stand firm is not a demand for grit; it rests on a promise about how the story ends.

Whom I love and long for. Six endearments in one verse, two of them the same Greek word, one near each end, so that the command is wrapped in affection on both sides. Paul is about to name two women in a public letter, and he first makes sure they know they are loved. “Long for” picks up the ache of 1:8.

My joy and crown. “Crown” (stephanos) is not the royal diadem but the victor’s wreath at the games. The runner of 3:14 tells this congregation that they are his wreath, the evidence on the last day that his labour was not in vain (1 Thessalonians 2:19–20). People are the prize.

Stand firm thus. “Stand firm” is the word of 1:27, a line of soldiers that holds when it is pushed. “Thus” gathers up the letter: stand firm like that, as citizens of heaven, in the Christ who has laid hold of you (3:12, 20). The command comes straight before the naming of a quarrel, because the two belong together: a congregation is seldom smashed by a persecutor from outside; it breaks along a seam that opened inside it.

The ground already taken. The ground under the line is Christ himself. He stood firm when every friend fled (Mark 14:50) and did not turn back from the cross. The believer stands not in his own resolve but in a Lord whose victory is finished, and his people hold because he holds them (John 10:28). And if an apostle could call a small, quarrelling church his crown, how much more does the Saviour delight in the people he bought with his blood.

What does standing firm look like in an ordinary week? Less like heroism than like staying put. Keep meeting with your church when you are tired or disappointed, holding to the gospel when clever voices would add to it (3:2), obeying where temptation presses hardest, and loving the believers next to you in the line, especially the difficult ones. And do it in the Lord, praying, remembering his promises and leaning on the people beside you: a line holds because each person stays where he is and trusts the one next to him.
verseByVerse.note: The “crown” is the victor’s wreath awarded at the games.

verseByVerse.quote: I entreat Euodia and I entreat Syntyche to agree in the Lord. Yes, I ask you also, true companion, help these women, who have labored side by side with me in the gospel together with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul pleads with two quarrelling fellow workers to be of one mind in the Lord, and asks a trusted colleague to help them. He takes neither side, and reminds the church that both women are gospel workers whose names are written in heaven.

Euodia and Syntyche. One of the very few New Testament quarrels where the people are named, and serious enough to reach Paul in prison (2:1–4). He does not say who is right or what the dispute was about. “I entreat” comes twice, once for each woman, so that no one hearing the letter read aloud could tell which of them Paul thought had started it.

To agree in the Lord. Literally, to think the same thing (to auto phronein) in the Lord: the exact phrase of 2:2, and the “mind” of 2:5. Paul asks not for the same opinion on everything but for the same attitude, Christ’s: not grasping, counting the other more significant. They can be reunited before the argument is settled, because they already have the same Lord.

True companion. Then he brings in a third person to help, which churches are slow to do. The word is syzygos, yokefellow, one of a pair of oxen pulling together (on who he may have been, see the end of this note). Most quarrels are left to sort themselves out, and harden; Paul assigns this one to a trusted person, in a letter everyone will hear.

Help these women. Before anyone can write them off as troublemakers, Paul tells the church who they are. “Labored side by side” (synathleō) is the athletic word of 1:27, contending together like a team. These were front-rank gospel workers, in a church that began among women at a riverside, with Lydia (Acts 16:13–15).

The book of life. That is Paul’s last word about them. Their names are in God’s register of his people, the citizens of heaven (Daniel 12:1; Luke 10:20), chosen in Christ by grace, not works (Ephesians 1:4–5; 2 Timothy 1:9). Among the names God wrote are a businesswoman, a jailer, two quarrelling women and a man called Clement whom history otherwise forgot. The quarrel is real, but their names in heaven are the deeper fact, and that is how a church should learn to see the people who exasperate it.

The Lamb’s book. Revelation calls it the book of life of the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 13:8; 21:27). The names are not there because the people were impressive, nor do they stay there because they behave well; they are there because the Lamb was slain for them. That is the deepest reason Euodia and Syntyche must be reconciled. Christ did not die to prove one of them right; he died for both, and a quarrel between two people he bought at the same price is a quarrel he has already paid to end.

What does this say about women’s ministry? Paul honours these women as fellow workers whose gospel work was real. He does not say what it was; nothing here suggests they were elders or preached in the church’s gathering, which Paul reserves for qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:2). This commentary holds that reading because Paul grounds it in creation rather than local custom (1 Timothy 2:13), while gladly recognising that many faithful Christians understand those verses differently. Women served the gospel in many ways in Paul’s churches, in hospitality, teaching women and children, supporting the mission and speaking of Christ, and a church that does not value and thank them as Paul did has not understood him.

I am at odds with someone in my church. Should others be involved? Begin privately: go to the person humbly, owning your part first (Matthew 5:23–24; 18:15). If that fails, ask one or two wise believers to help, as Paul asked his true companion, not to take sides but to help you both think the same thing in the Lord. Do not recruit supporters; that hardens a quarrel into a faction. Paul named these women because their quarrel was already public; most disagreements can be healed long before that stage.

How would I know whether my name is written in heaven? Not by trying to read heaven’s register, but by looking to Christ. Everyone who trusts him as Lord and Saviour was chosen in him (Ephesians 1:4). If you are trusting Christ, your name is there, and the evidence grows as you follow him: love for his people, desire to obey, grief over sin. If you are not yet trusting him, the invitation is open today.

Where Christians differ: can names be erased from the book of life? Some read Revelation 3:5 and Exodus 32:33 as showing that names once written can be blotted out, so believers may be lost; many earnest Christians hold this out of respect for Scripture’s warnings. This commentary’s view: the book of life records those chosen by God before the foundation of the world (Revelation 13:8; 17:8). Christ promises never to blot out the names of those who overcome (Revelation 3:5), and all true believers overcome (1 John 5:4). The names of God’s elect are written permanently, and this is the security in which Paul speaks of his fellow workers.

Uncertain wording. No one knows who the “true companion” was. Paul addresses someone the church would recognise at once. Suggestions include Epaphroditus, who carried the letter, Luke, Silas and a leading overseer. The word may even be a man’s name, Syzygus, with Paul saying that he lives up to it, though no one of that name is known from the period. Most likely he was a trusted leader in Philippi, so well known that no name was needed.
verseByVerse.note: The “true companion” is unnamed; some suggest Luke or Epaphroditus. The book of life is God’s register of his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — Rejoice, Do Not Be Anxious, and Mind What You Dwell On
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because the Lord is near, his people can live free of the grasping and the worry that drive everyone else. Rejoice in him always, and let everyone see your gentleness (vv. 4–5). Turn every anxiety into prayer with thanksgiving, and God’s peace will guard your hearts and minds in Christ (vv. 6–7). Fill the guarded mind with whatever is true, honourable and lovely (v. 8), and put into practice what you learned and saw in Paul, and the God of peace himself will be with you (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology:
Anxiety and Its Remedy

Verses 6 and 7 are the New Testament’s most direct treatment of anxiety, and the shape of the sentence carries the point: be anxious about nothing, but pray about everything. What is promised is not change but peace, arriving while the trouble is still there (this is treated fully at vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Philippians had ample material for anxiety: their apostle facing a capital charge, a quarrel inside the church, opposition outside it, and a future nobody could see. Paul offers no solution, but something to do (pray) and a promise (peace) while these remain unsolved.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice. Let your reasonableness be known to everyone. The Lord is at hand;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the Lord is near, his people can be glad in him at all times and gentle with everyone. Joy in Christ and a refusal to grasp are the climate in which a quarrelling church can heal.

Rejoice in the Lord always. Having said at 3:1 that he does not mind repeating himself, Paul repeats himself inside one verse: a man under a capital charge, writing to a church with a quarrel in it, says “rejoice” twice, because it is hard to believe and easy to forget. “Always” is possible only because of “in the Lord”. Joy that depends on circumstances cannot last; joy whose object is a Lord who never changes can be commanded without cruelty.

Reasonableness. Gentleness, forbearance, sweet reasonableness (epieikes). Aristotle used it of the judge who knows when the strict letter of the law would do an injustice: the person who does not insist on the last inch of what he is owed. Christ showed it, and Paul appeals to the Corinthians “by the meekness and gentleness of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:1).

The mind of chapter 2 in social clothing. Christ had every right and did not cling to it; the gentle person has a real claim and does not press it to the limit. Such gentleness is the Spirit’s fruit (Galatians 5:22–23), Christ’s own meekness grown in his people, and it is to be known to everyone: the neighbours, the magistrates, the pagan household next door. A church should be known in its town not for insisting on being right, but for not grasping.

The Lord is at hand. Two senses at once. Near in time: his return is coming (3:20; James 5:8), and if the Judge is on the road, you are free to stop prosecuting your own case. Near in presence: he is close to his people (Psalm 145:18), so you need not fight for your own corner. It is also the bridge to what follows: since the Lord is near, do not be anxious. The whole run of commands in verses 4–9 follows straight on from the quarrel (on the God of peace who ends it, see the note on v. 9).

Does this mean a Christian may not grieve, or must hide depression? No. Jesus wept at a friend’s grave (John 11:35), Paul tells us to weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15), and believers grieve, though not as those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Joy in the Lord is not a cheerful mood; it can sit beside tears, under them, as the settled knowledge that Christ is ours. A believer in depression has not failed this command. He may hold on to the Lord by a thread, and the joy is his even when he cannot feel it. If the darkness persists, he should talk to his pastor and a biblical counsellor, who will also ask him to have a medical check-up; medicine, where needed, is no failure of faith.

How can I be gentle when I am in the right? By remembering that being right does not require winning. Gentleness is not silence about truth; Paul has just called false teachers dogs. It is the refusal to press every claim, prove every point and repay every slight. Speak the truth in a tone that leaves the other person room, let small wrongs go, and ask whether insisting on your rights will help him or only satisfy you. The Lord is near; he will put right what needs putting right, so you do not have to.

verseByVerse.quote: do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Instead of carrying your worries, hand each one to God in prayer with thanksgiving, and his own peace will stand guard over your heart and mind in Christ. Paul does not promise that every problem will vanish, but that God’s peace will keep you while it remains.

Not anything, but in everything. The first clause alone would be unbearable: nobody has stopped worrying by trying. But the sentence is an exchange: everything you were going to be anxious about is moved, item by item, into prayer. Paul does not suppress the worry; he redirects it. The word for “anxious” is the one Jesus uses in Matthew 6:25–34 and to Martha (Luke 10:41): the mind pulled in many directions at once. Anxiety does not always feel like fear; often it feels like being unable to settle.

Prayer and supplication with thanksgiving. Prayer is the general word; supplication is asking for a definite thing, and that matters, because vague prayer relieves nothing, and the thing keeping you awake is never vague. Thanks, for past mercies and in advance for his answer, whatever it is, keeps asking from becoming a list of grievances read aloud to God. You cannot at the same moment thank him for what he has done and accuse him of not caring.

Made known to God. He knows them already (Matthew 6:8). The making known is not for his information; it is the act of handing over, done in words, because that is how a creature lets go of something: “casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). Much anxiety is the heart trying to hold what only God can hold: the future, other people, the outcome. Handing it over confesses that he is God and we are not, which is why it brings rest.

The peace of God. Paul does not say the circumstances will change, or the request be granted, or that you will understand why. He says peace will come: not only peace with God, which believers have through justification (Romans 5:1), but God’s own peace, the calm that belongs to him, given to us. It surpasses understanding because it is not the peace of a resolved problem but peace while the problem sits there unresolved: God keeps in perfect peace the one whose mind is stayed on him (Isaiah 26:3).

Will guard. A soldier’s word: to garrison a city.
